Temperament: ask a Vorthani why they are so calm and, if they answer at all: "Because I am so angry." They never say a thing twice.
Dress: a draped half-cloak edged in key-and-meander patterns, a wide sash, and wraps built for movement.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Vorthani First Ascent has taken in a guest who will not carry a stone. The monks say she is not a guest.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

illustration.alt: A stone-grey male Vorthani scholar and a muscular lilac-skinned female Vorthani in a martial stance, both with four arms, geometric markings and distinct horn shapes.
illustration.caption: A scholar and a martial artist of the Anvil Reach.

epigraph.quote: Finish what you begin. If you cannot finish it, do not begin it. If you began it anyway, carry it.

title: The Tarvan
subtitle: The horned clans of the high moors
summary: Herd-keepers, craftspeople, and champions for whom combat is an honored art.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Tarvan are broad, shaggy cattle-folk with sweeping pale horns, broad ears, kind bovine faces, and dark, long-lashed eyes. Coats range through russet, auburn, dun, black, and cream. Both men and women bear horns; the greatest champions and old bulls grow far beyond their already imposing kin.

sections.title: Horns and the locking
paragraphs: Horns grow throughout life. Brass, silver, and gold rings record deeds, children, droves, and vows. Breaking one is a grievous wound. To avoid kin-blood, many disputes are decided by the locking: horns set together until one yields.

sections.title: Herd-mother and hauld
paragraphs: The herd-mother leads in peace, judgment, and plenty. A chosen hauld leads the droving and rare wars. At the standing-stone moot all may speak, while children are fostered across the clan. Coming of age means a first droving and a first horn-ring.

sections.title: The warrior’s art
paragraphs: Heavy axes, mauls, and hammers are practiced with the care given to loom-work and song. Weapon-forms pass through generations. Patience and hospitality sit easily beside this disciplined mastery.

sections.title: Guest-law and the herd
paragraphs: A sheltered guest is sacred. Wealth is reckoned in cattle and kin; feuds are settled through raids, contests, compensation, marriages, and gifts. The flesh of a named beast or one of the clan’s own herd-line is forbidden.

sections.title: Cloth, stones, and the year
paragraphs: A clan’s tartan sett identifies its people. Songs preserve the dead, who lie beneath the standing-stones. First Grass, the Great Droving, and the Long Dark turn the year; the Gathering brings clans together for market, moot, song, and proving.

sections.title: Far-walkers and Saltmanes
paragraphs: Most Tarvan love their home moors and dislike the sea. The Saltmanes made mastery of navigation their tradition. Clans also bless their far-walkers, those drawn outward as Hunters, pilgrims, and wandering guardians.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Given names include Brae, Hamesh, Ferghus, Rauri, Mara, Senga, Rona, and Greer. Clan-names come first: Cravoch, Dunmor, Glenfask, Maccrenn, Brackmore, and Torroch.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Towering, shaggy, and horned, the Tarvan are the warmest of the big folk: patient, generous, slow to take offense, and stubbornly hospitable. Warmth is not weakness, though. Among the Tarvan, combat is an art, honored and perfected like weaving, brewing, or song, and a roused clan is a catastrophe.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: well past a human century; the eldest near two.

Faith: the Sleeping Giant and the clan-ancestors beneath the standing-stones, with a herdsman's wary respect for the beast-gods of the high country. The dead graze in the Endless Pasture, the Maghren, just beyond the stones.
To break or cut a Tarvan's horn is a grievous wound and a deeper shame.
Laws: guest-law above all, and the locking: quarrels are settled by setting horns together and shoving until one yields.
Dress: the clan's tartan (its sett) at the waist or shoulder, and wildflowers in the mane.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Tarvan on the Giant's Table heard the Sleeping Giant turn over in its sleep. She went home and sold every horse she had.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

illustration.alt: A russet-furred male Tarvan and a cream-furred female Tarvan stand side by side, with broad bovine faces, long ringed horns, clan tartan and shaggy coats.
illustration.caption: Two Tarvan among the standing-stones of the high moors.

epigraph.quote: A Tarvan doesn't hurry. A Tarvan arrives.

title: The Pocchin
subtitle: The market has arrived
summary: Fluff-furred merchants whose families are mobile, competitive, and wonderfully difficult to ignore.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Pocchin are knee-to-waist-high, round and extravagantly fluffy, with very long drooping ears, expressive little faces, thick fingers, and enormous plumed tails. Males are generally larger and heavier. Rings are displayed on neck-chains rather than fingers.

sections.title: The pride and the tail
paragraphs: A matriarch rules the traveling family; a dominant male is its loud public dealer. Only the matriarch and her direct daughters wear their tails loose. Others protect valuable growing fur in braids and silk wrappings or shear it for sale. A rare male keeping a full unshorn tail is making an extravagant declaration of wealth.

sections.title: The Fat Offer
paragraphs: Bargaining opens with a spectacularly lopsided offer. Laughing, spitting politely, and negotiating are expected. Once hands are shaken, the bargain holds; breaking it can close every caravan’s doors.

sections.title: Homes on living backs
paragraphs: Grommoth carry the houses, with roof goats above. At camp the houses are hoisted into trees or onto cliffs so the beasts can graze. No region owns a caravan route: families distinguish themselves by changing specialties and hard-won trade contacts.

sections.title: Sand and scent
paragraphs: Pocchin prefer fine sand-baths and submit reluctantly to the monthly water-shower. Their prized perfumery is a serious art. Family recipes are guarded, coveted, and stolen.

sections.title: Dress and names
paragraphs: Pocketed money-sashes, travel-scarves, brocade, ring-chains, bells, and silk favors are worn in generous layers. Ukin, Tobbin, Bram, Pobbo, Wuli, Dindle, Mungi, Nib, and Tatta are followed in trade by self-awarded titles of extraordinary length.

sections.title: A first coin, a first chain
paragraphs: Pocchin are born in litters of two to four, in the caravan-house on a grommoth’s back. The whole pride stops trading for the day, the only day it ever does. Every guest brings the newborns a first coin, and each kit’s first chain begins with those gifts.
Then comes the oldest caravan joke: a guest makes the family a Fat Offer for a baby, and the dominant male refuses at the top of his voice: not for all the Orsals in Goldwind.
The matriarch names each kit at its first sand-bath. The first fur combed from a kit is kept until it is old enough to weave its own piece of the family tapestry.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Pocchin are the wandering merchant-people of the archipelago, rolling from port to port in houses built on the backs of their great grommoth. They are adorable, they are revolting, they are the sharpest hagglers alive, and they will fight like cornered wolverines for what is theirs. Everyone loves them; no one fully trusts them; every wise crew keeps one close anyway.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about seventy to ninety years.
Look: small, round, enormous-eared, big-eyed, and fluffy past all reason. Rings strung on chains at the throat, because their fingers are too thick for them.
They are their caravans, and every caravan runs every route.
Faith: a cheerful magpie-creed borrowed from a dozen faiths and swapped without guilt; if a Pocchin prays, it is to whichever god seems likeliest to improve the next deal.
Family: a pride, led by a matriarch, with a dominant male who does the dealing.
Guests bring each kit a first coin to start its chain, and someone always makes a Fat Offer for the baby, which the family refuses at the top of its voice.
The family tapestry: every family keeps a tapestry of its generations, with a piece of each member's own fur added early in life and another at death.

Death: the Pocchin cremate their dead, to set them free. An elder or a Pocchin of note gets a great open feast that celebrates the life, and the tail is cut, dressed with jewels, and auctioned to the guests: the last deal.
Temperament: the Hoard is sacred. The opening Fat Offer is theater; the handshake is law. Break a struck deal and every caravan in the islands will shun you.
Habits: sand-baths, mud-wallowing, enormous meals, and constant, punctuating spitting. They regard water with deep suspicion.
Titles: bellowed, self-given, and stacked until no sane listener can keep a straight face.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Tobbin pride say Saffrane's famous Black Rose was theirs first, and that they still have the bill of sale.” (a Pocchin, loudly)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

illustration.alt: An ivory male Pocchin with a curled moustache and a cinnamon female matriarch, both round and fluffy, with extremely long drooping ears, enormous tails, brocade and jeweled chains.
illustration.caption: A prosperous merchant and a matriarch at a harbor market.

epigraph.quote: Triple the price, your boots, and naming rights to your firstborn. No? Fine. Let's talk.
epigraph.by: A Pocchin trader, opening a deal

title: The Sporrn
subtitle: The quiet folk of the under-dark
summary: Small fungal people whose colony life, strange stillness and skill in medicine make them unlike their neighbors.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Sporrn are Small. Living caps, heads, and shoulders grow into seamless fungal forms, without external ears. Dark eyes and blank expressions make their stillness both faintly endearing and unsettling. Pale tissue carries a dim inner glow.

sections.title: One self, never entirely alone
paragraphs: Each Sporrn is an individual, joined to its neighbors by the colony-link. Scent and spores carry thoughts, moods, alarms, and slow consensus; they do not dissolve the self. “We share our thoughts, not ourselves.”
Distance thins that belonging, making long travel lonely and uncommon.

sections.title: The bloom of the dead
paragraphs: The colony lets its dead bloom into new growth and new Sporrn. The Quiet Door is understood through rot becoming life, rather than a final ending.

sections.title: The deep trade
paragraphs: Their fungal pharmacy closes wounds, breaks fevers, and eases dying; the same careful craft makes subtle poisons. Metal, salt, and news are valuable exchanges. Old colonies keep quiet watch among drowned Orka places.

sections.title: Dress and names
paragraphs: Mycelium-felt grows into pale seamless robes. Fine spore-veils are a courtesy among other peoples. Names are humming tones tied to a place in the colony: Sel of the Quiet Ring, Ompo Third-of-Nine, Mirre of the Deep Shelf.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Sporrn are a fungal people of the dark Below, mushroom-fleshed and dim-glowing, each its own person, but linked mind to mind with its colony. They come to the surface rarely: to trade medicines and poisons, to flee something deeper, or out of a slow, spore-borne curiosity.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: a single Sporrn lives about sixty years; a colony lives for as long as it keeps blooming.
Look: pale, soft, and slow, mushroom-fleshed and faintly glowing.
Homeland: the deep caves and the drowned Orka undercities, the place the Orka called Nadhûr, and the colonies that keep watch over the Hollows.
Faith: no gods as the surface knows them; the endless turn of rot into bloom, the Quiet Door understood as compost for the next life.

The colony-link: not one mind, but many, linked. A Sporrn shares feelings, thoughts, and news with its colony, never its skills or its self. The link thins with distance and fades away far from the colony, and a Sporrn alone feels the silence keenly.
Who leads: whoever knows the matter best: the builder for building, the healer in sickness, the best talker with strangers.
Telling them apart: other peoples can hardly tell one Sporrn from another; Sporrn never confuse each other. Talk to two Sporrn on two days, and the second knows everything you told the first.

The Hollow Song: colonies near the buried Orka places sometimes begin to sing back to the wrongness below, and the song spreads along the colony-link like rot through fruit. Healthy Sporrn dread it above all.
Dress: mycelium-felt robes and deep hoods grown to fit, and fine-mesh spore-veils in company, as a courtesy.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Sporrn healer came up to Southhaven with medicine nobody asked for, three days before the fever arrived.” (heard in Southhaven)

facts: Fungal folk joined by the colony-link
source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

illustration.alt: Two Small Sporrn beside a human visitor for scale, with seamless fungal heads, broad living caps, no external ears, dark round eyes and blank expressions in a luminous cave apothecary.
illustration.caption: Small lives beneath the islands, quietly watching.

epigraph.quote: We share our thoughts, not ourselves.

title: The Coral Peoples
subtitle: The sea’s own
summary: Merfolk and their deep-court kin come ashore as pact-wardens, pearl-factors, and tide-pilots.

sections.title: The sea’s shore-lines
paragraphs: Merfolk and amphibious kin walk the ports as pact-wardens, pearl-factors, tide-pilots, and representatives of courts below. A resident Coral family means the deep is attending to a harbor’s conduct.

sections.title: Courtesy and the pact
paragraphs: Greet in song. Sound is a valued gift, and bare cold iron is a slur. The sea-pacts are sacred obligations whose terms connect each harbor to its neighboring court.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Ashore, quick-drying kelp-silk, shells, pearls, and netted half-cloaks are familiar. Wrist bells announce an arrival courteously. Underwater adornment is grown: cultured pearls, trained coral, and light-bearing life.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Nereth, Sirae, Ondine, Selka, Murro, and Thessa. The court replaces a surname: Sirae of the Glass Gardens, Murro of the Whispering Current.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The coral peoples are the deep courts' children who can walk dry land: the fair folk of the Glass Gardens, the twilight secret-traders of the Whispering Current, and the grave keepers of the Grey Fathoms. A port with a coral family in residence is a port the deep is watching.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: two to three centuries.
Homeland: the deep courts beneath the sea, and the shore-lines of the ports they keep pacts with.
Faith: the Drowning Mother, and the old powers of their court.
Temperament: courteous, musical, and patient as tide. They never forget a broken pact, and they never forget a kindness either.
Bynames: the court stands in place of a family name, as in Sirae of the Glass Gardens.

sections.title: Playing one of the coral peoples
paragraphs: Why you came ashore: you are a pact-warden sent to watch a port, a pearl-factor on business, a tide-pilot for hire, or an envoy the court would rather not admit it sent.
Classes that fit: bard, druid, warlock of a court's old patron, cleric of the Drowning Mother.
Backgrounds that fit: Pearl Diver, Tidecaller Acolyte, Factor.
Heritage feat: Court Envoy.

Hooks: a sea-pact your port is about to break; a drowned friend the Grey Fathoms will not give back; the Red Choir singing in a harbor where it should not be. (The Red Choir and the Sunken Thrones are not playable courts.)

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A court envoy came ashore at Easthold with bells on both wrists and asked to speak to whoever keeps the harbor's oldest promise.” (heard in Easthold)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

illustration.alt: A female and male amphibious Coral envoy with pearlescent sea-green skin, gills, fin-edged ears, webbed feet, kelp-silk, pearl ornaments and wrist bells.
illustration.caption: Shore-walking envoys at the harbor’s water steps.

epigraph.quote: The surface is so loud. How do you hear each other think?
epigraph.by: A Glass Gardens courtier on her first visit ashore

title: Lampet
subtitle: The harbor’s smallest light
summary: A cat-sized, buoy-round harbor companion with velvet fur, long white whiskers, and a glowing Krysta brow-star.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: The size of a well-fed cat and round as a buoy: a seal-pup's body with an otter's cleverness, dense velvet fur that sheds water like oil, mottled slate-blue to kelp-brown over a cream belly, huge dark eyes, and long white whiskers that curl forward when it is pleased. It slaps the water twice with its flat paddle tail before every dive, the lampet's knock. In its brow sits a natural fleck of Krysta, the brow-star, which glows soft cyan at dusk and flares when the lampet is excited. Every lampet's light is faintly its own, and harbor children know theirs by the glow alone.

sections.title: Its gift
paragraphs: It dives for anything dropped over the side and brings it back. Sailors swear on their mothers that it keeps every tenth coin: the lampet's tithe.

sections.title: Earning its trust
paragraphs: You don't. A lampet adopts a ship or a dock on its own and nests in the coiled rope. Feeding it helps. Arguing with it does not.

sections.title: In island life
paragraphs: It floats on its back holding a favorite pebble.
It honks, foghorn-loud, at weather the glass has not caught yet, and sailors trust the honk over the glass.
At dusk the harbor lampets line the pilings and glow: the lighting of the lamps.
A ship with a lampet aboard is lucky. Harming one is the fastest way to be beaten senseless in any tavern in Kalvatar, and the magistrate will hear the case with visible reluctance.
Lampets come in regional kinds:
Shaggy and storm-grey in the Northern Frontier.
Gold-dusted in the Gilded Shallows.
Round and snow-white on the ice.
Sleek and near-black among the Coral peoples, with the brightest stars of all.
The chant-keepers call lampets the Mother's smallest lights, meaning the Drowning Mother, and feed them accordingly. So does everyone else, just in case.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: "Lampets remember a face for thirty years."

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A lampet in Greyhaven brought up a gold ring nobody aboard had lost, and the harbor-master's wife has been very quiet since.” (heard on the Greyhaven docks)

illustration.alt: A storm-grey lampet holds a holed copper Bit on a foggy Frontier dock at night, its cyan brow-star shining above a coil of rope.
illustration.caption: The harbor’s smallest lights gather on the pilings in the fog.

gallery.alt: An ink-and-watercolor Lampet field-guide plate on warm paper, with brow-star and copper Bit studies, a sailor’s boot for scale, and a harbor-work vignette.
gallery.caption: A naturalist’s studies of the brow-star, the lampet’s tithe, and the lighting of the lamps.
gallery.label: Lampet: field guide

epigraph.quote: Lampets remember a face for thirty years.
epigraph.by: What people say in the harbors

title: Lantern Mouse
subtitle: Its tail-light, which it lights or puts out as it pleases.
summary: A brown field-mouse with oversized ears and a tail that ends in a soft, warm glow, like a coal seen through a paper screen.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A brown field-mouse with oversized ears and a tail that ends in a soft, warm glow, like a coal seen through a paper screen. Lantern mice live in granaries, mills, and the lofts of lighthouses, and for as long as there have been windows in the islands, they have been sitting in them.

sections.title: Its gift
paragraphs: Its tail-light, which it lights or puts out as it pleases. A lantern mouse in a coat pocket is the cheapest lamp in Kalvatar.

sections.title: Earning its trust
paragraphs: The Sill. Leave a little food on the windowsill beside a covered lamp for three nights running. On the fourth, there is a mouse in the window, and it is yours.

sections.title: In island life
paragraphs: Fishing families set a lantern mouse in the window while someone is at sea, so the Answering Light is never wholly dark.
Children who are afraid of the dark get a mouse before they get a candle.
Delvers like them because the glow is small and steady, and does not draw what a naked flame draws Below.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: "Leave a light for the mouse." (Keep the house open for someone who is late.)

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The lighthouse keeper at Saltreach swears her mouse put its tail out the night a ship went by with no lights at all.” (heard in a Frontier tavern)

facts: Granaries, mills, and lighthouse lofts; most common in the Central Heartland

illustration.label: Lantern Mouse
illustration.alt: A brown field-mouse with oversized ears and a tail that ends in a soft, warm glow, like a coal seen through a paper screen.
illustration.caption: A brown field-mouse with oversized ears and a tail that ends in a soft, warm glow, like a coal seen through a paper screen.

epigraph.quote: Leave a light for the mouse." (Keep the house open for someone who is late.)
epigraph.by: What people say in the harbors

title: Pocket Rainfrog
subtitle: It keeps things dry.
summary: A plump brown frog the size of an egg, freckled like a river stone, with a mouth turned permanently down in disapproval of the weather.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A plump brown frog the size of an egg, freckled like a river stone, with a mouth turned permanently down in disapproval of the weather. Rainfrogs came out of the Southern Wilds in the holds of trading ships and spread up every lane, because they do one thing nobody else can.

sections.title: Its gift
paragraphs: It keeps things dry. Whatever it sits on stays dry through rain, spray, and a quick dunking, and so does what is inside.

sections.title: Earning its trust
paragraphs: In Storm Water, build one a shelter of a broad leaf. If it likes the work, it climbs onto your shoulder. It always picks the wettest person present.

sections.title: In island life
paragraphs: Couriers of the Chartwrights' Guild carry one in every chart-satchel, so the charts arrive dry. In any port, carrying frog means a courier.
It croaks at the sky about an hour before rain. Washerwomen hang their washing by it.
A rainfrog on a scholar's book-bag means a scholar who has lost a book to the rain before.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: "Ask the frog." (Said before planning anything outdoors.)

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A courier's rainfrog sat on a Council dispatch through a whole shipwreck. The dispatch was dry. The courier was not so lucky.” (heard among Harbinger crews)

facts: Everywhere along the trade lanes; first came out of the Southern Wilds

illustration.label: Pocket Rainfrog
illustration.alt: A plump brown frog the size of an egg, freckled like a river stone, with a mouth turned permanently down in disapproval of the weather.
illustration.caption: A plump brown frog the size of an egg, freckled like a river stone, with a mouth turned permanently down in disapproval of the weather.

epigraph.quote: Ask the frog." (Said before planning anything outdoors.)
epigraph.by: What people say in the harbors

title: Button Badger
subtitle: It finds what is lost.
summary: A small, striped, short-legged badger, never bigger than a loaf of bread, with clever black paws and a settled belief that buttons are the most valuable things in the world.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A small, striped, short-legged badger, never bigger than a loaf of bread, with clever black paws and a settled belief that buttons are the most valuable things in the world. Every button badger carries one button, usually bent, and it will trade that button for a better one.

sections.title: Its gift
paragraphs: It finds what is lost. It always knows where the nearest loose button is, and it can find a small thing its person dropped that day.

sections.title: Earning its trust
paragraphs: Offer a shiny button for the bent one it carries. If it takes the trade, it follows you home, and it brings you a different button every time you come back to camp.

sections.title: In island life
paragraphs: The halflings' luck-charm, a button borrowed from a friend, began as a badger's trade. A halfling who carries a badger's button is twice lucky.

Kobolds love button badgers and button badgers love kobolds, and nobody knows what they talk about. Tailors keep a dish of spare buttons by the back door for the badgers, which is cheaper than having them come in.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: "Trade up, like a badger." (Do better, a little at a time.)

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Somewhere below the coral there is a reef made entirely of buttons, and every button badger in the islands knows the way.” (a tailor's back door)
“A button badger in Silverport keeps bringing home silver buttons with a house crest nobody can place.” (heard in a Silverport tailor's shop)

facts: Hedgerows, gardens, and tailors' back doors everywhere

illustration.alt: A small, striped, short-legged badger, never bigger than a loaf of bread, with clever black paws and a settled belief that buttons are the most valuable things in the world.
illustration.caption: A small, striped, short-legged badger, never bigger than a loaf of bread, with clever black paws and a settled belief that buttons are the most valuable things in the world.

epigraph.quote: Trade up, like a badger." (Do better, a little at a time.)
epigraph.by: What people say in the harbors

title: Teacup Moth
subtitle: It warms a drink.
summary: A soft, fat moth with wings patterned like a good tea-service, cream and rust and faded blue, and a body as furry as a kitten's ear.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A soft, fat moth with wings patterned like a good tea-service, cream and rust and faded blue, and a body as furry as a kitten's ear. Teacup moths love warmth but never fly into a flame, and they love a full cup best of all.

sections.title: Its gift
paragraphs: It warms a drink. A teacup moth folds its wings over a cup or a pot like a blanket, and in a minute the drink is just warm enough, and stays that way.

sections.title: Earning its trust
paragraphs: Leave a saucer of sweet brightleaf on the sill at dusk. A moth that comes back three evenings running settles on your mug for good.

sections.title: In island life
paragraphs: Every halfling teahouse has a few, and brightleaf warmed by a moth is the mark of a good house.
Night-watchmen, lighthouse keepers, and the Armada's midwatch swear by them.
Delvers say the teacup moth is the surface cousin of the lightdrinkers Below. These give warmth. Those take light.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: "Keep a moth on it." (Keep something warm for someone coming late.)

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “They say a teacup moth will not warm a cup that has been poisoned. Nobody has been brave enough to test it twice.” (heard in a Goldwind teahouse)

illustration.alt: A plush cream moth folds its rust-and-blue patterned wings over a teacup on a harbor-side table.
illustration.caption: A Teacup Moth at work: cream, rust, and faded blue wings folded over a cup like a blanket.

epigraph.quote: Keep a moth on it." (Keep something warm for someone coming late.)
epigraph.by: What people say in the harbors

title: Aurocs
subtitle: Everyday mounts and towering giants
summary: Flightless riding and working birds from Assios. Everyday aurocs are the size of a large horse; great aurocs stand two or three storeys tall.

sections.title: Scale and bearing
paragraphs: An everyday auroc is about the size of a large horse: a flightless bird suited to ordinary riding and daily work. Its plumage can range through many colors.
Great aurocs are the true giants, standing two or three storeys tall. That immense scale belongs to the great auroc, rather than the regular riding bird.

sections.title: Domestic and great aurocs
paragraphs: Regular domestic aurocs are steady work animals with longer beaks, used to haul, plough, carry, and take riders. Great aurocs are war-birds first, with heavy, flatter beaks, vivid plumage, and an aggressive bearing. They also carry heavy loads.

sections.title: North and south
paragraphs: Most arrive along the Crown Route into the Northern Frontier. They are associated with the great houses and the imperial-descended north, while saurians are the characteristic mounts of the native south. A Jakupur noble riding an auroc is making an expensive point.

sections.title: The cost of prestige
paragraphs: A domestic auroc costs 150–300 Anchors; a great auroc begins at 500. Raising one builds loyalty. Moving a great auroc between islands demands a very large merchantman and an expensive berth.

sections.title: Passage by sea
paragraphs: A domestic auroc travels below decks in a horse-stall. A great auroc needs the hold of the largest merchantmen, and an expensive berth.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The auroc is a great flightless bird from the continent of Assios, a living engine of transport and war. It holds a cruising pace three times a galloping horse's, bursts twice as fast again in a charge, and hauls a laden war-wagon. Their plumage comes in every color under the sun.

sections.title: The two breeds
paragraphs: Domestic aurocs are the workhorses: slimmer, longer beaks, even tempers, and tremendous strength.
A trained one is a terror on a battlefield, and great aurocs also carry the heaviest loads.

sections.title: Aurocs in the islands
paragraphs: Saurians are the mounts of the native south, and a Frontier noble on a great auroc and a Jakupur rider on a swordtooth are two halves of an argument about who Kalvatar belongs to.

sections.title: As a companion
paragraphs: An auroc is not a pocket companion, but a rich adventurer can ride one, and an auroc is loyal to the rider who raised it. The full account of the breed is in Volume VI.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A great auroc broke its tether at Bastion and walked straight to the Tarvan moors, as if it knew the way.” (heard in Bastion)

facts: The size of a large horse

gallery.label: Great Auroc
gallery.alt: A crested great auroc towers two or three storeys above an adult keeper at the harbor.
gallery.caption: A crested great auroc towers two or three storeys above an adult keeper at the harbor.

gallery.caption: The chain rises before the afternoon is dark.

title: Saurians
subtitle: The mounts of the native south
summary: Twenty named saurian kinds shape the Southern Wilds, from household flocks and racing mounts to towering haulers and rarely tamed predators.

sections.title: Two names for every kind
paragraphs: Common compounds describe a trait and defining feature: Swift-crest, Sword-tooth, or Murk-strider. Kalvatari names preserve the older southern words. Both are used.

rows: Placid long-necked freight and plough beast
The tallest domesticated hauler and platform
Broad herd-grazer for meat, hide, and eggs
Small dangerous predator with paired crests
Elegant herbivorous mount with a resonant crest
Herbivorous pack saurians of several breeds for long journeys
table.caption: The twenty named saurian kinds

sections.title: The Eldersaur title
paragraphs: Tza’kun, the revered ancient, names an Eldersaur. It is a title for an exceptionally old, enormous saurian, rather than a separate breed. Even Jakupur leaves many such territorial giants alone.

sections.title: Jakupur and the bond
paragraphs: Breeding-lines, taming traditions, and lifelong bonds make Jakupur the center of the saurian trade. Tana Sukuun’s stables are famed; her rose-grey Dreadmaw is Old Thunder. Her brother Teoma represents Sukuun among the Twelve Flags.

sections.title: Food, work, speed, and display
paragraphs: The trade spans meat and eggs, labor, war, racing, materials, and rare display animals. Saurians lay eggs and give no milk; southern dairy still comes from mammals.

Herbivorous saurians serve distinct needs. Songcrests are valued as elegant riding animals, while Loadbacks carry expedition baggage and caravan goods over long routes. Those uses sit alongside the great hauling work of Loambacks and Altisaurs and the food herds of Bellowbacks.

sections.title: The Sunspine Run
paragraphs: Swiftcrest racing fills the great track outside Jakupur. Sissix-the-Comet, the silver-crested champion, is known throughout the circuit. A noble importing an auroc into this world is making a costly cultural statement.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, The Saurians; Bible Lite · §§3, 8

epigraph.quote: The north rides birds. We ride what the birds are afraid of.

illustration.alt: Saurian riders and fruit sellers move through Jakupur’s wet stepped streets above a jungle river.
illustration.caption: After rain, the White Flame watches the streets steam.

title: Hands and Whiskers
subtitle: Everyone has someone small.
summary: Across the islands, companions make difficult lives a little easier. A good captain counts a crew in hands and whiskers.

sections.title: Someone small
paragraphs: A companion is an ordinary living creature with one small useful gift. It chooses a life beside a person: keeping a coal alive, a letter dry, or a watch through the dark. A crew is counted in hands and whiskers.

sections.title: The five everywhere
paragraphs: Lampet, Lantern Mouse, Pocket Rainfrog, Button Badger, and Teacup Moth are known in every port. Each has a particular way of choosing a keeper.

sections.title: A bond, not merchandise
paragraphs: Most companions are won or given. Selling one that chose you is an insult to the bond. A few species, including counting jackdaws, are bred and sold; gifts such as promise doves follow their own customs.

sections.title: At the family table
paragraphs: Companions are fed before the guests. A child’s first companion is named on the back of the Naming Spoon. When one dies, it is buried beneath the doorstep so it still knows the way home.

sections.title: A working animal has its own life
paragraphs: A Lodge Hound is assigned by a Lodge, a chartback passes through its trade, and a grommoth belongs to a caravan. Many useful beasts cannot simply be bought or carried away.

sections.title: What a companion is
paragraphs: A companion is not a pet kept for show, and not a familiar called up by a spell.
Most islanders have one, and many adventurers have at least one.
Some can only be given. A few, like the counting jackdaw and the aurocs, are sold, and dearly.
Ask a captain how many aboard, and a good one tells you both.

sections.title: Customs
paragraphs: A companion that chose you is never sold. To offer to buy someone's companion is an insult, and to accept is worse.
Harming a lampet is the fastest way to be beaten senseless in any tavern in Kalvatar.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Goldwind noble offered a fortune for a street child's mirror plover. The child said no, and the plover said something worse.” (heard in Goldwind)

epigraph.quote: How many aboard? Sixty hands, and eleven whiskers.

title: The Charter Calendar
subtitle: A year read as a voyage
summary: Ten months, five Still Days, two moons, and seasons named for the sea.

sections.title: The shape of a year
paragraphs: A Charter year has ten months of 36 days, followed by five Still Days that belong to no month. The present year is 175 EC. Dates take a god’s name, as in Liora 18th, 175 EC.

table.caption: The ten months of the Charter year

sections.title: The four waters
paragraphs: Closed Water is winter, Open Water spring, Fair Water summer, and Storm Water autumn. The Wilds follow rains and dry seasons, while the ice reverses the seasonal pattern.

sections.title: The Still Days
paragraphs: During the five days between Okram and Eo, debts pause and courts close. Fae bargains fall due. The ten-day Cycle continues through them without resetting.

sections.title: The ten-day Cycle
paragraphs: The Cycle continues across month boundaries and through the Still Days. Tideturn is a day for sailing, Graveday is not; Coinsday brings markets and Restday rest.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The months are named for ten gods and the part of life each keeps. You write the date with the god's name: Liora 18th, 175 EC.
The islands name their seasons for the sea:
In the Wilds there are only the rains and the dry, and on the ice everything runs the other way round.
The Still Days are festival days when debts pause, the courts close, and every fae bargain in the islands comes due.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A hush owl went quiet at a wedding in Saltreach last Storm Water, and the groom has not been seen since.” (a Frontier tavern)

epigraph.quote: Ten months to work, five Still Days to forgive.

title: The King Tide
subtitle: The Three Nights
summary: Roughly every third year, the moons and Ors align and the sea rises beyond its usual bounds.

sections.title: Three days and nights
paragraphs: Low shores drown and reefs and ruins emerge. The Savage Lords stir, deep things rise, and the Veil to the Faewild thins. Sensible households stay behind warded doors.

sections.title: The next alignment
paragraphs: The last King Tide occurred in 174 EC. The next is expected in 177 EC, though Tidecallers publicly dispute the week. Once in a generation, the greater alignment called the Deep King redraws coastlines; the next is reckoned for 180 EC.

sections.title: How the islands keep the Three Nights
paragraphs: Every port closes, and a ship caught at sea is on its own.
Families ward their doors and stay inside. The Tidecallers keep vigil on the harbor walls.
Harbor children chalk the morning's high-water line on the harbor steps: the Chalk Tide. That is how they learn the moons.
The sea uncovers reefs and ruins no one has seen in three years, and floats boats over places they could never cross.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Tidecallers agree on the year and are publicly arguing over the week. Coastal land is quietly changing hands.
The Tidecallers reckon the next for 180 EC.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Captain Blackstorm: he once outmaneuvered the whole Armada during a King Tide.” (the docks, about the Most Wanted)

epigraph.quote: By the Three Nights, stay home. Ward the door. Let the sea have what it wants.

title: Orsals and Anchors
subtitle: What the islands call money
summary: Bits, Tides, Anchors, and the heavy gold Orsal keep trade moving between regions that give common coins their own names.

rows: Silver; two moons over a wave
Gold; an anchor over a running wave
Heavy numbered square of gold; the face of Ors
table.caption: The islands’ common coinage

sections.title: A measure of a living
paragraphs: Everywhere, the Orsal remains the Orsal. Familiar yardsticks put a laborer’s day at three Bits, a month around an Anchor, and a year around an Orsal. A journeyman earns about two Anchors monthly; a clerk three; a master craftsman four to six.

sections.title: Credit and the Still Days
paragraphs: A reckoning is a letter of credit issued through the Reckoners. The Still Days freeze every debt. An unpaid obligation can follow its owner through the Ledger just as surely as a ship follows a chart.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Bit: copper, with a hole in the middle for stringing. Thirty on a cord make a string, a laborer's Cycle.
A counterfeit is a drowned Anchor.
It pays for ships, dowries, land, and ransoms, and most people never hold one. Old folk still call it a sun.
A Bit buys a fishbread, a mug of ale, or a cup of brightleaf.
Merchant captain: 15 to 30 Anchors.
Fleetlord: 100 Anchors.
Magic is never a catalog. A market town has one or two worked pieces for sale, if any. Goldwind has dozens. Every legal sale pays the Registry's tenth.
Two makes: everything ordinary comes in harbor make, local and cheap, and proof make, guild-stamped and about ten times the price.
Coinsday is settling day everywhere.
Off the coin-roads, people barter:
Salt and iron nails on the outer Frontier.
University scrip among Goldwind's scholars.
Cacao beans, jade beads, saurian teeth, and worked feathers in the deep Wilds.
Whale-oil, dried fish, and furs on the ice.
Pressed leaf-bricks of brightleaf aboard ship.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The new Tides are lighter than the old ones. The Mint says it is the wear of the dies.” (heard on the Spire Floor)

source: Bible Lite · §8; Bible Complete · Volume XXI

epigraph.quote: A Bit for bread, a Tide for wine, an Anchor for a month of work. An Orsal? Nobody I know has seen one.

title: Passage Between Islands
subtitle: The map is measured in weeks
summary: Voyages and news move slowly across the enormous archipelago.

sections.title: What changes the journey
paragraphs: A fast hull cuts a third from the passage. A convoy adds a third. The King Tide closes ports. These are fair passages, not guarantees against weather, damaged rigging, or the unexpected.

sections.title: A distant government
paragraphs: A journey from the Frontier’s tip to the far ice takes five to six months. News travels in months too, and the regions largely govern their own daily lives.

sections.title: Hulls with a purpose
paragraphs: A ship’s class tells an islander what it has come to do. The Armada’s vessels range from courier cutters to the great ships of the battle line.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: News travels in months; the Council's writ travels slower; the regions largely run themselves.
Never set sail on a Graveday.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Harbinger made Ironfort to Goldwind in eleven days. The Admiralty will not say how.” (heard in Ironfort)

epigraph.quote: Six months tip to tip, if the sea is kind. The sea is never kind.

title: The Small Ways
subtitle: Magic in a tea-stained notebook
summary: Tiny hearth-workings that sweeten cups, thread needles, and make daily life a little kinder.

sections.title: The everyday craft
paragraphs: The Small Ways are the little workings passed between families and kept in waybooks: sweetening tea, drying nets, finding a lost button, calling fireflies to a windowsill or lending a lullaby a gentle warmth. They sit beneath the nine circles. Knowing them alone requires neither enrollment nor a copper ring.

Their place is the ordinary life of the islands. A small kindness may reach another person, an animal or a plant. A Way must remain harmless, modest and free of compulsion. Scholars call them residual spillage of true casting; the Concord calls them the world’s small kindnesses; the hedge-wives call them Tuesday.

sections.title: The Three Refusals
paragraphs: The refusals describe the nature of the magic. A kindly intention cannot make a harmful effect into a Small Way.
A Way harms no one. It cannot injure, poison, spread illness, damage another’s belongings or deprive another of what is theirs. It cannot prepare a harmful effect to be triggered later.

A Way compels no one. It may offer comfort or make an invitation perceptible, but cannot impose obedience, affection, trust, sleep or silence. A person or creature can ignore it, refuse it or leave. Helping a baby settle with a soothing lullaby is possible; forcing the baby asleep is not.

A Way wins no contest. It provides no advantage in fighting, pursuit, coercion, gambling or another consequential challenge. It cannot conceal an attack, lure a creature into a trap, defeat a lock or make someone accept a bargain. A harmless coin trick may delight a table, but it cannot decide a wager.

sections.title: A call, freely answered
paragraphs: A firefly-call is an invitation carried through a little light or a familiar rhythm. Nearby fireflies may approach, remain where they are or wander away. The Way neither summons insects from nowhere nor takes control of them. It cannot compel them to follow a route, reveal a hiding place or enter danger.

The same distinction applies to other living things. A little warmth may comfort a willing neighbor. A garden Way may help keep a pot comfortably watered. Neither can force a feeling, cure a fever or turn a seed into a grown tree. Permission to touch life does not give the Small Ways the scale of true spells.

sections.title: Small effects, ordinary measures
paragraphs: A Small Way can last through an evening, keep a household measurement, count visitors at a gate or help a small account add up. Ordinary numbers and durations are allowed. Their scale remains domestic, and repeated workings cannot be stacked into a greater spell.

At the table, a Small Way requires no roll, grants no bonus and replaces no consequential check. Use it freely for small tasks and moments of character. When an effect would settle a contested outcome or overcome an adventure’s obstacle, it exceeds the Small Ways.

A sheathed sword nearby, a passing worry or an ordinary swell at sea does not extinguish household magic. Drying a sailor’s shirt aboard a peaceful voyage is a fitting use. Holding a mast together in a storm, strengthening a weapon or silencing footsteps past a guard exceeds its nature.

sections.title: The waybook
paragraphs: Alongside a spellbook, many mages carry a small, fat, tea-stained waybook. Grandparents, sailors and household craftspeople keep them too. The margins hold corrections, recipes and warnings in several generations of handwriting. A treasured book may still smell of someone’s grandmother’s kitchen.
A Way for a Way: copying from another’s waybook is done by invitation, usually in exchange for a working of one’s own. Uninvited copying is considered petty theft and terrible luck.

The waybook is never registered. Its last page stays blank for the Way its keeper has yet to learn. Filling that last page is taken as an unsettling announcement that one expects to learn nothing more.

sections.title: Triflings
paragraphs: Wandering casters trade their year’s silliest workings at little fairs called Triflings. The grand prize is a wooden spoon and eternal glory. Serious mages sneer in public and attend hooded. A new ribbon trick or a particularly considerate teapot can travel from port to port in the margins of a dozen waybooks.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A grandmother in Sunhold has a waybook whose blank last page has started filling itself in.” (heard in Sunhold)

facts: Household tasks, comfort and harmless wonders
No harm, compulsion or advantage in contests
source: Kalvatar Small Ways; Welcome to Kalvatar; Kafeii’s clarification on harmless effects and freely answered calls · 175 EC

epigraph.quote: Call the fireflies. Let the fireflies decide.

illustration.alt: A grandmother shares a tea-stained waybook in a seaside kitchen as fireflies approach the window.
illustration.caption: A Way for a Way, passed over tea and thread.

title: Krysta
subtitle: The crystal that runs the age
summary: A rare spell-bearing crystal found chiefly in Kalvatar; the purest and most valuable unimbued stones are flawlessly clear.

sections.title: Purity and the spell inside
paragraphs: The finest Krysta is completely clear before it is imbued: no natural color, veins, flecks, bubbles, or clouding anywhere inside. Its clarity is prized above all other grades. An included stone may still be worked, but it is not the most valuable kind.

When a spell is imbued, its color appears within the transparent crystal. The working can be seen unfolding in its depths, a spectacle that makes a finished piece as fascinating to watch as it is useful. The color belongs to the spell, not to the untouched stone.

sections.title: Focus and battery
paragraphs: Alone, Krysta is inert. As a focus it strengthens a caster’s magic. As a battery it holds a stored spell that someone else can release. Larger stones carry stronger workings; better craft preserves them for longer.
Size determines how much a stone can hold; the quality of its workmanship determines how long it holds it. Purity is a separate measure of the stone itself.

sections.title: Where it is found
paragraphs: Kalvatar holds the deposits that built its crystal trade, especially the Darlath mines beneath Everfall and the southern workings near Karn Sorroch. Krysta has also been found beyond the archipelago, but deposits there are scarce and their quality varies. An outside source does not make every foreign stone inferior; it does not end the islands’ hold on the trade.

sections.title: The hands behind it
paragraphs: Krystawrights are known to mages and noble houses by their own names and by the family whose workshop employs them. A renowned craftsperson can be as coveted as the flawless stone on the bench.

Their guild belongs to the Mercantile Congress. Some masters run entire workshops devoted to training apprentices. A few houses and workshops try to lure outstanding talent away from rivals; many others refuse to play that game.

sections.title: Law and value
paragraphs: Registered Krysta is legal and expensive. Unregistered dark glass is another matter. Its rarity and usefulness make it central to the archipelago’s power and to the mainland’s interest in the islands.

sections.title: Beyond the Veil
paragraphs: Krysta does nothing in the Faewild. The familiar rules of an island workshop do not travel everywhere.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Size is capacity: a small stone holds about one first-circle working; the next size up, one second-circle working or two of the first.
Craft is duration: a refined stone leaks its spell in days; a masterpiece holds it indefinitely.
The tiers: raw, refined, worked, and masterpiece.
Dark glass is unregistered Krysta, not a color or a purity grade; it costs one and a half to three times as much as registered material of comparable grade.
Glint is the Undertow's drug: Krysta-dust snuff, wild magic, and glassed eyes.
Where it comes from: the Darlath mines under Everfall, refined in the Heartland; raw Krysta from Karn Sorroch and the Vossreth mines in the south.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Midnight Patron has been buying every old chart of the far south, and paying in uncut Krysta.” (a Zal'Kareth chart-seller)
“One crate of Darlath stone in twelve leaves Everfall marked 'broken' and is never seen at the refinery.” (an Everfall carter)

facts: Completely clear; no color, veins, flecks, or bubbles
The spell’s color is visible inside

epigraph.quote: On its own, it's a pretty pebble. In the right hands, it's a war.

illustration.alt: A Krystawright inspects a flawless clear unimbued crystal beside another holding a vivid spell inside its transparent body.
illustration.caption: The finest stone has no color of its own. The color comes from the spell within.

title: The Faewild
subtitle: Count every bargain three times
summary: Beyond the Veil, names, debts, and promises carry a weight no visitor should underestimate.

sections.title: Rules every child hears
paragraphs: Never give your true name. Never say thank you, because it acknowledges a debt. Never accept a gift you cannot repay. Count a bargain three times before agreeing.

sections.title: Tides and debts
paragraphs: The Veil grows thin at the King Tide. Fae bargains come due during the Still Days, and Krysta does nothing across the threshold. Preparation is useful; careless certainty is not.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Everyone knows the rules:
Summer, the Burning Crown, under Pyraxis, the Unbowed Flame.
Autumn, the Red Harvest, under Vael Mournthorn, the Crimson Reaper-King.
Winter, the Long Silence, under Morthryn, the Pale Empress of Air and Ending, who exiled the Frost Elves.
Spring, the First Bloom, under Aoifel, the Green Laugh.
The Unbound, who belongs to no court, and whom the four courts fear.

epigraph.quote: Count every bargain three times, and then once more.

title: The Sea-Pacts
subtitle: A harbor is an agreement
summary: Ports bargain with the deep courts for safe water, warnings, and the return of their drowned.

sections.title: What the shore gives
paragraphs: A port offers the first catch of each season, the true names of its ships, and burial rights over those lost at sea. These obligations bind the harbor to the court whose waters it uses.

sections.title: What the deep gives
paragraphs: In return come safe water, storm-warning, and the drowned returned. Breaking a pact can drown a harbor’s luck. A traveler’s quiet voyage may depend upon an agreement made long before their ship arrived.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Coral Kingdoms are the courts beneath the sea: merfolk, sahuagin, and stranger kin, older than the Firstborn. Like the Fae, the sea-peoples are of two natures: the Sunlit Courts, the bright sea, beautiful, warm, and more often than not kind; and the Sunken Courts, the dark sea, ancient, alien, and patient.
The Glass Gardens: fair merfolk; living reef-architecture; memory-pearls.
The Whispering Current: twilight secret-traders; the currents carry every word spoken over water.
The Grey Fathoms: the kept drowned; ransom of the dead.
The Red Choir: the sahuagin blood-faith; they sing when blood is in the water.
The Sunken Thrones: the midnight abyss.
The Old Shells: leviathan sage-turtles; three questions a generation.
Ports keep pacts with the courts:
Break a pact and the harbor's luck drowns.
Etiquette: greet the sea-folk in song, any song; effort counts. Give them gifts of sound: bells and music-boxes. Never show them bare cold iron.
The Coral Sovereign Vaythra rules over the Sunlit courts. About one Kalvatari in forty depends on a sea-pact.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A memory-pearl sold in Pearl Groove shows a woman's face on the Sunken Thrones. She is looking up, and she is smiling.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

facts: A port and a deep court

epigraph.quote: A harbor is an agreement. Break it, and the harbor's luck drowns.
epigraph.by: A Tidecaller of the Last Psalm

illustration.alt: A harbor elder offers the first catch and a sealed list of ship names to merfolk emissaries at the waterline.
illustration.caption: A port renews its bargain with the sea.

title: Guest-Law
subtitle: A bowl before a question
summary: Across Kalvatar, hospitality is a serious obligation with different expressions in each region.

sections.title: The Frontier and the south
paragraphs: On the Frontier, the stranger is fed before being questioned. In the south, a guest seated at the heart-fire is under protection.

sections.title: The ice and the mountain
paragraphs: Refusing a traveler food and fire on the ice is murder. At a Vorthani Ascent, an arriving traveler is owed broth, warmth, and a bed, with no questions until morning. The guest pays by carrying a stone before leaving.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Slavery is illegal in Council lands, and has been since the Great Slave Rebellion. It survives, illegally, in the south.
The Gate-Tithe: one Tide in every Anchor on goods entering or leaving through the Frontier.

Salvage law: drowned goods are not free goods. The Reckoners register claims on named wrecks, the Chartwrights on new finds, and the Coral courts on anything in pact-water. Every dive is also a legal heist.
Letters of marque make privateering legal, until the Navy decides it's awkward.
The Registry: copper rings, or trouble.
Charts: a chart is legal only with a Chartwrights' stamp. A forged stamp is a hanging.
Justice differs by region:
Martial and swift on the Frontier.
In the south, native chant-keepers and colonial courts disagree about everything.
On the ice, hold-law, blood-feud, and exile.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gate-Tithe is cheating us in both directions. It keeps the gold in Ironfort and sends the paper to Goldwind.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)

epigraph.quote: A bowl before a question. Always.

illustration.alt: A Frontier household offers hot food to a rain-soaked traveler by the hearth.
illustration.caption: On the Frontier, a stranger is fed before being questioned.

title: Below
subtitle: The dark under the islands
summary: Miners and sailors speak carefully of the caves and old roads that join the islands beneath the seabed.

sections.title: What people say
paragraphs: Everyone knows there is something under the islands, and few care to name it. Caves run through the roots of drowned mountains. A draft that follows the tide is called Below breathing.

sections.title: The traveler’s warnings
paragraphs: Stop your ears with wax. Mark every turning. Shutter the lamp. Never say a name Below, and never say one twice. Above all, never sing back.

sections.title: Rumor, not a chart
paragraphs: Kobolds and Sporrn are known in the depths, and miners swear the drow live farther down. Surface accounts are warnings and rumors, not a reliable survey of the dark.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: It floods at the King Tide and redraws its caves at the Deep King.
No Charter, Chartwright stamp, or registered claim reaches it, and the Lodges post no contract behind a wall or through an Orka door.
It has three names, one for each depth, and it is bad luck to say them:
Kharzûm, the dwarves' word; say the Unpaid. The galleries under the holds, behind walls marked do not open until it is paid.
Nadhûr, the Orka word; say the Swallow or downstairs. Drowned undercities behind black doors carved with a barred mouth, found even where the Orka never ruled.
No elf will translate it.
The dwarven luck-load: the twelfth load of every shift is tipped down the deepest shaft.
Who lives down there: kobold warrens, Sporrn colonies that grow living seals over the old doors, the Savage Lord Ulgrenn singing in the dark, and, the miners swear, the drow.
The Gullet: a Fogrunner tide-cave out of Black Harbor.
The Cistern Door: a dwarven wall under Goldwind's oldest cistern.
The Knot: the one market Below, under Duskmire, kept by goblins.
The Ember Roads: lava tubes under Everfall, broken open by the Darlath diggers in 172 EC.
Golgarma's Throat: the great Orka stair, held by the Crimson Legion since 175 EC.
The Flame Gate: under Jakupur, sealed by the Sacred Flame.
The Rime Ways: channels under the winter sea-ice of the Expanse.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Masons in seven dwarven holds have stopped talking about what they found on the shelf beside the wall.” (a dwarven mason's apprentice)
“The dwarves have an old word for the drow, and they will not say it in front of a banker.” (a Goldwind money-changer)
“The dry road. The roads Below run island to island, and a smuggler who knew them could walk a cargo from Black Harbor to Goldwind without paying a single harbor due.” (common talk)
“Somewhere below the coral there is a reef made entirely of buttons, and every button badger in the islands knows the way.” (a tailor's back door)

epigraph.quote: Two rules down there. Carry more light than you think you need. And never answer a voice you didn't hear first up here.

illustration.alt: Travelers with a shuttered lantern approach an ancient barred-mouth door in a flooded cavern Below.
illustration.caption: The old doors wait beyond the tide line.

title: The Savage Lords
subtitle: Their progeny, never the Lord
summary: Colossal beast-gods whose territories and moods shape the lives of the communities around them.

sections.title: Living powers
paragraphs: Villages leave tribute at the borders of a Lord’s territory to buy another season of peace. The first rule of the wild is simple: fight a Lord’s progeny, never the Lord itself.

sections.title: Names the islands know
paragraphs: Momumba is Lord of Apes; Badron the Queen of Feathers; Kayuntu the Violent Monarch of the Five Skies. KakanKal is the Emperor of Flames below Everfall. Malim is the Laughing Flood; Ssvayuk the Mud That Breathes; Vukharr the White Hunger.

sections.title: The older warnings
paragraphs: Shakarr belongs to the Bonewilds. Thalgorath is the Tide-Tyrant of the deep. Ulgrenn is the Hollow Song: if you hear it, do not follow. Tyrak’Zhul is called the World-Eater, the First Jaw.

rows: A cunning colossal girallon with a cohort
The mother of storms and thunderbirds
Kayuntu, the Violent Monarch of the Five Skies
The five layers of the sky
A fire salamander asleep in the magma
A giant otter, playful and lethal
A swamp-serpent grown over with false islands
A starving god of ribs and white fur
The deep caves and Orka ruins
The saurian heartlands of the south
A young beast the Lords' progeny unite to kill
table.caption: Ten and a half, and the eleventh.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The educated of the University call them Apex Primordials; the natives, the Old Beasts; sailors, the Jungle Lords.
Progeny are the lesser beasts that share a Lord's nature and territory, and Hunters track them for glory and materials.
The King Tide makes them stir.
There are ten and a half known Lords, and the eleventh. The half is the Hunted, a young apex that the others unite to kill.
Their names are known everywhere.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Progeny of three different Lords were seen hunting side by side in the Southern Wilds, all chasing the same pale animal.” (heard at the Jakupur Lodge)

epigraph.quote: Fight the progeny. Never the Lord.
epigraph.by: The first rule of the wild

illustration.alt: Momumba, a colossal white four-armed girallon, bares his canines above a jungle acropolis whose ruined towers fit beneath his hands.
illustration.caption: The jungle has a throne.

title: Council of the Charted Isles
subtitle: Five seats, a charted sixth
summary: The Council governs from Goldwind under a Charter first signed at Ironfort.

sections.title: The five seats
paragraphs: The Nobles are represented by Halsof Varselis, the Hunters by Lactinius Windcaller, the Mercantile Congress by Horace Goldspire, the Navy by Arios Fafner, and the University by Thessaly Kane.

sections.title: The reach of the Charter
paragraphs: Roughly one island in six falls under the Council’s authority. Distance, old custom, and months-long passages make the regions more independent in practice than a Goldwind writ may suggest.

sections.title: Power outside the chamber
paragraphs: The Concord has no seat and needs none. The Reckoners’ Hall, guilds, and noble houses exercise influence through duties and obligations that are not confined to a Council vote.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: In the Island tongue, the word means both the chart and the charter.
Halsof Varselis is young, ambitious, and calculating, and often seems colder than he is.
Lactinius Windcaller is charismatic, unpredictable, and beloved by the city. His colleagues tolerate the chaos because no one knows the archipelago's dangers better.
Horace Goldspire is pompous, ostentatious, and indispensable.
Arios Fafner rarely attends in person. Alina Fafner carries his views on security and defense, and has begun to bring her own.
Thessaly Kane succeeded her father, Thobias Kane, as head of the University. The old headmaster still advises her from his library.
The Council's writ travels slower than its ships.
The Chartwrights' Guild licenses surveys and pays hard coin for verified charts.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The empty chair in the Admiralty's High Command was dusted last week. Nobody admits to ordering it.” (heard among Goldwind clerks)

epigraph.quote: Five seats, and every one of them is sure it's the important one.

illustration.alt: The Council debates an island chart in Goldwind, with the exceptionally beautiful platinum-blond elf Lactinius Windcaller seated beside the merchant representative.
illustration.caption: Five seats. One sea between them.

title: The Hunters
subtitle: The Ledger of Deeds follows you
summary: Escorts, explorers, and monster-slayers whose origins lie in guarding the Exodus convoys.

sections.title: A Lodge in every chapter
paragraphs: A Lodge is led by its Lodgemaster and a Board. The Contract-Master posts work, the Quartermaster equips it, and the Chronicler keeps the Ledger of Deeds that follows a Hunter between houses.

sections.title: Bronze to Platinum
paragraphs: Bronze marks initiation after the Trials of Ascension and the Oath. Silver Hunters are proven and vote at Lodge moots. Gold Hunters are masters. Platinum are the Ten, whose identities are secret; Lactinius is the only publicly known Platinum.

sections.title: An iron is not a rank
paragraphs: Only 300 iron endorsement coins are struck in a year. A candidate needs a current iron to sit the annual Trials. The coin gives a chance to attempt them; it is not a Hunter rank. The founding house and mint is the Crucible in Ironfort.

sections.title: Titania and the Iron Swan
paragraphs: Titania, captain of the Iron Swan, is a Gold Hunter, eleventh in the Ranking. She has been the top Gold for eight years.

sections.title: The price of a contract
paragraphs: The Lodge takes a tithe of one Anchor in ten. Platinum contracts are never posted.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Hunters, or the Hunter's Guild, are the guild of escorts, explorers, and monster-slayers. They were founded at Ironfort in the first year of the Charter, and their tradition goes back to the guards who fought for the Exodus convoys.
Its chapter-houses are Lodges, each run by a Lodgemaster and a Board:
The Goldwind Lodge is the principal house.
Work: contracts on the Board are legal and modestly paid; unposted Grey Market work pays double and costs standing if it surfaces.
Sponsors: houses and firms sponsor crews like racing stables.
The Ranking: a public popularity ranking of Hunters is followed like a sport.
The only known Platinum is Lactinius Windcaller, who sits for the Hunters on the Council and is their face at every public act.
The Armada is their friendly rival: see the Breakwater and the Charter Match.
The Code, spoken at the Vow and at every Hunter's burial:

We stand between the dark and the hearth, and we do not ask whose hearth it is. We fight for those who cannot, and we ask no thanks for it. We keep our word: to the client, to the crew, and to the dead. We carry one another, whatever it costs, as far as the road goes. From iron to platinum, we fight as one.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Platinum Ten walk among us. Nobody knows who they are.” (common talk)
“The first of the Ten has held the top of the Ranking since before anyone's grandmother was born. The Chroniclers stopped writing down her age.” (a Lodge Chronicler, after his third kellum)
“A giant of a Frost Elf walks the ice with a hooded priest who never eats. The Hunters posted a contract on him, and Albion Tempest took it.” (a Frosthold Lodge clerk)

facts: An endorsement coin, not a rank

epigraph.quote: We do not turn back. We do not run. From iron to platinum, we fight as one.

illustration.alt: Three Hunters bring an injured adult traveler safely to a northern Lodge, each wearing their own rank-and-branch Sigil: an orc Warrior, a human Scout and a halfling Mage.
illustration.caption: As far as the road goes.

title: The Kalvatar Armada
subtitle: Nine fleets, a thousand obligations
summary: The Council’s navy binds the charted isles by patrol, convoy, oath and force. Under Grand Admiral Kalivos Durant, its nine fleets each keep a different part of an immense sea.

sections.title: A navy between islands
paragraphs: The Kalvatar Armada, the KAN, began when the early island communities pooled their ships against pirates, sea-beasts and one another’s raids. Taelon Stormrider, its first Grand Admiral, bound those vessels into a single fleet. The present navy has grown into nine fleets, each with its own Fleetlord, charge and flagship.

Its work stretches from the Crown Route to the Icy Expanse, from southern rivers to the Coral Kingdoms. A patrol protects a passage; a rescue brings people home; a blockade closes a route. For islanders whose roads are made of water, naval decisions reach well beyond the quarterdeck.

sections.title: The Admiralty’s table
paragraphs: Grand Admiral Kalivos Durant, Lord of the Nine Fleets, commands from the Conqueror and keeps the First Fleet, the Iron Wall. Lady High Marshal Serane Marr is second in the Armada and First of the Ivory Command. Storm Marshal Brigid Thane heads the Cerulean Vanguard; Lord Castellan Edran Holst oversees ports, stations and fortifications.
A fifth chair is officially empty. On the docks it is called Shroud’s chair.

sections.title: A coat and a place aboard
paragraphs: Every recruit begins in grey and earns a color. Blue Coats are the Cerulean Vanguard, the fighting line. White Coats belong to the Ivory Command, the strategists and diplomats. Black Coats are the Ebon Blade, charged with infiltration and sanctioned covert work. Branch and rank are separate parts of an officer’s position.

A ship has its own working offices. The Oathwarden keeps discipline and oath; the Sword-Warden serves as master-at-arms. A Tidecaller blesses the sailing, the Master of Thunder leads the guns, the Chartmaster navigates and the Rook watches from the top. Knowing a hull means knowing the people who make it work.

sections.title: What a hull has come to do
paragraphs: A Harbinger cutter carries news; a Vindicator sloop gives chase; a Justicar gunboat takes naval force into a river. Warden frigates form the backbone of the fleets. Beyond them stand storm-running Juggernauts, blockading Interdictors, the Dreadnought battle line and the Enforcers built to bombard fortresses.

Only nine Executioner men-of-war were built. Their number does not assign one to every Fleetlord: Falken Brightsight still commands from the Falkoner he fought at the Kraken’s Maw, and the Far Watch famously flies no Executioner. Ship Classes of the Armada sets out the whole range; The Nine Fleets follows their commanders and waters.

sections.title: Names, oaths and the first drop
paragraphs: The Armada remembers Lyanna Seaborn as the pirate-breaker and Orin Thalas as the admiral who rebuilt the fleet. Larissa Whitewave was its first admiral risen from the lower deck; her example opened the way for the Blooded to rise.

Its Sailor’s Oath binds honor, duty and loyalty to the islands and their people. At a commissioning, a bottle of kellum breaks on the bow so the sea takes the first drop. The daily ration is the Charter’s tot. At a sea burial, the dead person’s name is spoken once before they are given to the deep.

sections.title: The cost of crossing orders
paragraphs: At the Breakwater in 91 EC, an Armada quarantine writ and a Hunter rescue contract collided. A refugee ship crossed the line in fog; an hour of fighting left two hundred wounded and thirty-one dead. Larissa Whitewave and the Gold Hunter Odran Halloway rowed between the lines unarmed. The refugees were healthy.

The Breakwater Protocols now require conflicting Armada orders and Hunter contracts to stand down and go before the nearest Council officer. The annual Wargames in Veriden practice joint maneuvers, escorts and boardings, then close by reading the thirty-one names. The public Charter Match is a separate, friendlier expression of the rivalry. At the Kraken’s Maw, the two orders fought together for the islands’ survival.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Captain Blackstorm once outmaneuvered the whole Armada during a King Tide.” (a dockside account of the Most Wanted)
“Siroc the Swift has escaped the Armada more than a dozen times.” (heard on the docks)

epigraph.quote: A Harbinger means news, and news is rarely good.

illustration.alt: Blue Coat sailors help a fisherman from a pitching boat during a cold squall, with a brown-hulled Warden frigate standing by on the grey-green sea.
illustration.caption: An archipelago to protect.

gallery.alt: Brigid Thane, Serane Marr, Kalivos Durant and Edran Holst confer over the Admiralty's sea chart, with the fifth chair visibly empty.
gallery.caption: Four voices. Five chairs.
gallery.label: The High Command

title: The Concord
subtitle: The Risen Sun and the Deep Tide
summary: The religious institution whose temples and sea-priests touch lives throughout the islands.

sections.title: Sun, sea, and order
paragraphs: The Concord honors harmony among the gods of sun, sea, and order. Its Tidecallers bless fleets, read the moons, and broker sea-pacts. The Sunward Alesse Brightwater and Tidecaller Ondrel Greywake lead it.
Ondrel Greywake is an old sea-priest of Easthold, who read the moons for the Last Psalm for thirty years.

sections.title: The weight of an oath
paragraphs: Its faceless Pursuers are said to hunt those who break great oaths. Even the Armada gives them room. The Concord holds no Council seat, but few powers cross it lightly.

sections.title: The unresolved registry
paragraphs: The Concord refuses to register its casters with the Arcane Registry. The tension is part of the islands’ public religious and political life.

sections.title: The faith in practice
paragraphs: The Concord's creed is Piety, Harmony, and Justice. Its Sunward priests keep the temples and give the law its moral weight; its Tidecallers bless the fleets, read the moons, and broker the sea-pacts with the deep courts.

The Grand Temple in Goldwind rises over the city's heart, its great sun-and-tide window catching the morning. Every Armada ship carries a Ship's Tidecaller, and one whole fleet, the Last Psalm, is the Concord's own.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Nearly everyone prays at its temples, and no faction crosses it lightly.
Its altars stand to Law the Sun King, Okram, Tholmar, Lilim, Eo, Halvenir, Veriden, and the rest of the gods of sun, sea, and order.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gilded Shallows are glowing at night now, even when the tide is low. The Concord says it is a blessing. The Registry says it is a fire.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“The Red Choir has started singing on a quiet night, when there is no blood in the water. The Tidecallers say the song is coming up the Starfall Reef.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“A Pursuer came to Southhaven hunting an oath-breaker, and the man she took away was a whaler who could not stop humming.” (a Southhaven harbor-widow)

facts: Concord of the Risen Sun and the Deep Tide
Sunward Alesse Brightwater; Tidecaller Ondrel Greywake
aliases: Concord of the Risen Sun and the Deep Tide

epigraph.quote: Sun for the land, tide for the sea, and harmony between them, or nothing at all.

illustration.alt: A Tidecaller blesses a young sailor's voyage inside Goldwind's Grand Temple while a Sunward priestess speaks with the sailor's family beneath the sun-and-tide window.
illustration.caption: Harmony between them.

title: The Chartwrights’ Guild
subtitle: A verified chart is worth coin
summary: Surveyors and chart-keepers turn uncertain passages into knowledge someone else can sail by.

sections.title: Charting the islands
paragraphs: The Guild licenses surveys and pays for verified charts of islands, routes, and hazards. In a world where islands can rise or vanish, a chart is a record that needs revisiting.

sections.title: The stamp
paragraphs: A Chartwright’s stamp on a map carries real value. Forging one is a hanging offense. Couriers often carry pocket rainfrogs so the charts entrusted to them arrive dry.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Chartwrights' Guild licenses every survey in Council waters.
It pays hard coin for verified charts of new islands, passages, and hazards. A Chartwright's stamp on your map is money; a forged one is a hanging.
Its last census counted more than 5,800 islands, "wrong in both directions every year."
Under salvage law, the Chartwrights register claims on new finds.
The Armada's Sixth Fleet, the Far Watch, writes the world's map with them.
Most of the map is blank. Most of what's on it is wrong. Somewhere out there is an island no one has charted, and the Chartwrights will pay you for it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Chartwrights keep the tortoise islands off the public charts. Ask a surveyor where they are and watch his tortoise look at him.” (a Goldwind chart-shop)

epigraph.quote: A line on a chart is a promise. Never draw one you haven't sailed.
epigraph.by: A Chartwright master to an apprentice

title: The Mercantile Congress
subtitle: The islands’ work, counted
summary: The collective of trade guilds, from shipwrights and smiths to weavers and longshore dockers.

sections.title: Guild and Council
paragraphs: Horace Goldspire represents the Congress on the Council. Its guilds organize the trades that move goods and sustain ports across the archipelago.

sections.title: The Reckoners and the Flags
paragraphs: The Reckoners’ Hall is its bank, under First Reckoner Maera Blackstrand. The Twelve Flags are the merchant families whose posts stand on the Goldspire Exchange’s Spire Floor, where commodity prices are called each Coinsday.

sections.title: Beyond the guilds
paragraphs: The Charterhouse Company stands outside the guild structure, with Council-chartered monopolies and its own company towns and enforcers. Trade is never just the exchange of coins.

sections.title: The Krystawrights
paragraphs: The Krystawrights’ Guild belongs to the Congress. Its masters cut, set, and work Krysta for mages and great houses. The finest crystal is clear until a spell is imbued; the skill and reputation of the person working it can make the commission as desirable as the stone.

Apprentice workshops train new hands, and some rival patrons compete fiercely for the most gifted. The guild represents this trade; the University’s Arcane Registry separately regulates the practice of higher-circle magic.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Shipwrights of Goldwind and the Vanris yards.
The Stillwrights, who make kellum.
The Cartographers' Compact: charts are legal only with a Chartwrights' stamp.
The Brine Brotherhood, the fishers and whalers.
The Longshore, the dockers; their Goldwind boss is Morgha Wall-Holder.
The Terrace Guild, the brightleaf growers.
The Perfumers of Silverport, at open war with the Pocchin.
The Saurian Handlers' Lodge of Jakupur, an associate.
The cargo chain: grower, factor, warehouse stamp, a Reckoners' bottomry bond, the Holst customs seal, convoy or Hunter escort, then market. Every stamp has a forger.
The Krystawrights’ Guild, whose celebrated masters are known by patron house as well as by name.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Two of the Twelve Flags have stopped speaking to each other on the Spire Floor, and every factor in Goldwind is buying rope.” (heard on the Spire Floor)

epigraph.quote: The Council makes the laws. The Congress makes the money. Guess who wins the argument.

title: The Krystawrights’ Guild
subtitle: The hand behind the crystal
summary: A celebrated guild of Krysta artisans within the Mercantile Congress, whose masters are prized by mages and noble houses.

sections.title: Stone and spell
paragraphs: Krystawrights sort, cut, set, and finish Krysta for commissions across the islands. The most coveted unimbued material is utterly clear, with no color, vein, fleck, or bubble. When a spell is worked into it, that spell’s color can be seen within the crystal.
