illustration.alt: A pod of wild orcas, black and white and clever, which has hunted beside the whalers of Frosthold for generations.
illustration.caption: A pod of wild orcas, black and white and clever, which has hunted beside the whalers of Frosthold for generations.

epigraph.quote: When the wolves slap the water outside the harbor, run for the boats.

title: Strider Crab
subtitle: The Coral peoples use it to carry cargo between the courts and the market harbors of the coast.
summary: A giant spider crab with legs longer than a man is tall, which walks along the seabed with baskets lashed to its back.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A giant spider crab with legs longer than a man is tall, which walks along the seabed with baskets lashed to its back.

sections.title: The work
paragraphs: The Coral peoples use it to carry cargo between the courts and the market harbors of the coast.

sections.title: What it tells you
paragraphs: In ports that trade with the courts, Coinsday begins when the crabs walk up out of the surf, loaded with baskets.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: Only for a Coral character, and it tires quickly on land.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A strider crab walked out of the sea at a market harbor with no rider and a basket full of bells.” (heard on the Heartland coast)

facts: The Coral Courts, and the market harbors that trade with them

illustration.label: Strider Crab
illustration.alt: A giant spider crab with legs longer than a man is tall, which walks along the seabed with baskets lashed to its back.
illustration.caption: A giant spider crab with legs longer than a man is tall, which walks along the seabed with baskets lashed to its back.

epigraph.quote: It walks the seabed with the market on its back.

title: Tidesteed
subtitle: It is the mount of the Coral peoples, for travel and for war.
summary: A seahorse the size of a horse, the bubble seahorse's giant cousin, with a fluted crest and a saddle of shell.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A seahorse the size of a horse, the bubble seahorse's giant cousin, with a fluted crest and a saddle of shell.

sections.title: The work
paragraphs: It is the mount of the Coral peoples, for travel and for war.

sections.title: What it tells you
paragraphs: A surface-dweller riding one is a guest of the courts, and everyone below knows it.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: Only underwater, and only with the courts' leave.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A tidesteed with an empty shell saddle has been seen off Easthold three nights running.” (heard in Easthold)

illustration.label: Tidesteed
illustration.alt: A seahorse the size of a horse, the bubble seahorse's giant cousin, with a fluted crest and a saddle of shell.
illustration.caption: A seahorse the size of a horse, the bubble seahorse's giant cousin, with a fluted crest and a saddle of shell.

epigraph.quote: A tidesteed is not ridden. It agrees to go somewhere with you.

title: Lamp-Shoal
subtitle: They light the streets of the coral cities.
summary: Shoals of small glowing fish, blue-green and gold, trained by the Coral peoples.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Shoals of small glowing fish, blue-green and gold, trained by the Coral peoples.

sections.title: The work
paragraphs: They light the streets of the coral cities. Every shoal swims the same round every night.

sections.title: What it tells you
paragraphs: From a ship on a moonless night, you can sometimes see the streets of a court glowing under the water.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: No.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “One lamp-shoal in Thalassar has started swimming a new round, and the courts are arguing about where it leads.” (heard among pearl divers)

facts: The streets of the coral cities

illustration.label: Lamp-Shoal
illustration.alt: Shoals of small glowing fish, blue-green and gold, trained by the Coral peoples.
illustration.caption: Shoals of small glowing fish, blue-green and gold, trained by the Coral peoples.

epigraph.quote: Every night, the same round, so nobody in the coral cities is ever lost.

title: Reefpurple Whelk
subtitle: The Coral peoples farm it in reef pens.
summary: The sea snail that gives reefpurple, the rarest dye in the islands.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: The sea snail that gives reefpurple, the rarest dye in the islands.

sections.title: The work
paragraphs: The Coral peoples farm it in reef pens. Each whelk gives a single drop of dye, which is why a vial costs thirty Anchors.

sections.title: What it tells you
paragraphs: The dyers of Pearl Groove have purple hands for life. By custom, only the Council's seats and the high clergy of the Concord wear reefpurple; anyone else who wears it is making a claim.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: No.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Someone is selling reefpurple dye in Silverport at half the price. The Coral peoples want to know where it comes from.” (heard in Silverport)

facts: The reef pens of the Coral peoples, and the dye-works of Pearl Groove

illustration.label: Reefpurple Whelk
illustration.alt: The sea snail that gives reefpurple, the rarest dye in the islands.
illustration.caption: The sea snail that gives reefpurple, the rarest dye in the islands.

epigraph.quote: One whelk, one drop. That is why the purple costs thirty Anchors.

title: Haulbeetle
subtitle: The islands' working lives
summary: A beetle the size of a pony, with a dull black shell, short strong legs, and a placid appetite for rock-moss.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A beetle the size of a pony, with a dull black shell, short strong legs, and a placid appetite for rock-moss.

sections.title: The work
paragraphs: Dwarves use it to drag ore carts through the tunnels, and the mines of the Northern Frontier use it too.

sections.title: What it tells you
paragraphs: Miners wear shoulder-guards cut from the shells the beetles shed.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: Yes, for someone who goes Below often. It needs no light.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A haulbeetle in a dwarven tunnel stopped and would not move, and the miners found a door behind the rock it stopped at.” (heard in a dwarven hold)

facts: The dwarven tunnels, and the mines of the Northern Frontier

illustration.label: Haulbeetle
illustration.alt: A beetle the size of a pony, with a dull black shell, short strong legs, and a placid appetite for rock-moss.
illustration.caption: A beetle the size of a pony, with a dull black shell, short strong legs, and a placid appetite for rock-moss.

epigraph.quote: It pulls the cart, and it knows when the roof is about to fall.

title: Chartback Tortoise
subtitle: Good charts are drawn at tortoise pace.
summary: A handcart-sized tortoise carrying the instruments, records, or remedies of three traveling trades.

sections.title: A keeper older than the master
paragraphs: Chartbacks live well past a hundred and fifty years. Their shell plates look like islands; people say each is a chart of an undiscovered shore. Apprentices are assigned to a tortoise, rather than the other way around.

rows: A green cross of bound reeds
table.caption: The three chartback trades

sections.title: Shell-keeps
paragraphs: A plain load is carried in saddlebags. Grand ones sit in little wooden shell-keeps: roofed towers with scroll cubbies or herb drawers, handed down with the tortoise. A surveyor measures land in the animal’s remarkably constant paces; a notary’s chartback can walk its circuit without being led.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: A chartback passes to its keeper’s apprentice or trade hall and is never sold outside the three trades. An adventurer might inherit one or take in a retired animal. Villagers are likely to assume that the newcomer has arrived to measure their land.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A giant tortoise as big as a handcart, slow, patient, and almost always older than its keeper.

sections.title: More on Chartback Tortoise
paragraphs: A chartback works for one of three trades, and if you see someone walking beside one, you know at once what they do.

The land-surveyors of the Chartwrights' Guild walk the islands to measure them, and a chartback carries their instruments and chart-cases. Its stride does not change in a hundred years, so the Guild measures land in tortoise paces.
When a surveyor's tortoise comes up the road, every farmer goes out to check his fences.
The notaries who walk a circuit of villages, under Veriden's oath, carry sealed wills, deeds, and contracts on the shell.
The tortoise wears a little scholar's cap.
When a notary's tortoise comes up the road, someone is about to sign something, or someone has died and someone else is about to inherit.
The traveling healers of Maela the Mender carry their herbs, salves, and spices on the shell, so a healer's tortoise smells like a spice market from twenty paces.
A green cross of bound reeds hangs at the front of its load.
A healer's tortoise goes where the fever is, and villages open the gate before it knocks.

sections.title: What they carry
paragraphs: Every trade dresses its tortoise differently, and the loads are half the pleasure of seeing one.
The plain loads are leather sacks strapped on like a horse's.
The grand loads are small wooden towers, two or three storeys high, each storey with its own little roof whose eaves curl up at the corners, like a lord's keep the size of a wardrobe.
Notaries and surveyors stand their scrolls upright in the shell-keep's cubbies, so nothing creases.
Healers fill its little drawers with herbs and spices.
A good shell-keep is made by a joiner who makes nothing else, and it is handed down with the tortoise.

sections.title: The tortoise and its trade
paragraphs: In the three trades, an apprentice is assigned to a tortoise, not the other way round. The tortoise has seen more islands than the master.
A notary's tortoise knows its circuit and walks it without being led.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “An old chartback in Goldwind has a shell whose plates match an island no chart shows. Three surveyors have asked to buy its charts. It is not for sale.” (heard among the Chartwrights)

illustration.alt: A handcart-sized Chartback Tortoise in a sun hat carries a wooden scroll-keep beside a barefoot surveyor in loose cream trousers.
illustration.caption: A surveyor’s Chartback, carrying chart-cases and instruments in a small wooden shell-keep.

epigraph.quote: Good charts are drawn at tortoise pace.

title: Grommoth
subtitle: A house on a living back
summary: The huge, shaggy, horned beasts that carry the Pocchin’s walking caravan-houses.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A full-grown grommoth is the size of an elephant and broad enough to fill a street: a placid mountain of long, shaggy hide and horn, something between a buffalo and a rhinoceros, with the strength of a barge. Wood, hide, and salvage become a cluttered little home on its back.

sections.title: The caravan at rest
paragraphs: When the caravan camps, pulleys lift the houses into trees or onto cliff-faces, leaving the beasts free to graze. Roof goats travel above; one grommoth carries the great tubs of sand used for Pocchin baths. Each animal flies its own flag and title.

sections.title: What a caravan owes
paragraphs: Wool becomes felt and blankets; milk becomes a strong yellow cheese. When an old beast dies, a feast both mourns and celebrates it. A Pocchin will sell what a grommoth makes, but never the grommoth.

sections.title: Keeping one
paragraphs: A grommoth belongs to its caravan. A Pocchin adventurer may bring a calf only with the caravan’s blessing, and is expected to bring it back fat and happy.

sections.title: Grommoth and caravan
paragraphs: On every roof rides a goat or three. The Pocchin love goats almost as much as they love their grommoth (see the roof goats).

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Pocchin family turned down a whole island for their oldest grommoth. Twice.” (heard in a caravan camp)

facts: Elephant-sized; broad enough to fill a street

illustration.alt: An elephant-sized, four-legged Grommoth with a very shaggy russet coat carries a caravan-house, beside two small lop-eared Pocchin and a barefoot adult human for scale.
illustration.caption: An elephant-sized Grommoth with its Pocchin keepers and a human islander for scale. The caravan-house rides on a padded harness; a roof goat travels above.

epigraph.quote: A Pocchin will sell you anything but this.

title: The Dragonborn
subtitle: Clan before self
summary: Mainland scale-folk who cross the strait as refugees, exiles, and traders of the long war.

sections.title: A mainland inheritance
paragraphs: Dragonborn carry the formality of Assios with them, whether they preserve it or deliberately reject it. Clan and duty matter deeply; an oath is taken slowly and held firmly. Kobolds often greet them as distant dragon-kin, an unsolicited kinship most bear with weary grace.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: High-collared mainland coats are fitted around scale and crest, with clan-colors at the sash. Some remove imperial insignia and wear the visible stitch-marks as a declaration.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Korrath, Sazkhan, Merrash, Ilzara, and Ozreth. Clan comes before self in importance: Korrath of Clan Ossarim.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The dragonborn crossed the strait from Assios in the long war, and they carry the mainland in their bearing: imperial formality kept out of habit, or defied with equal precision. They are clannish, dutiful, and slow to swear, and once sworn they do not break.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about eighty years.
Look: scaled, crested, and tall, with the color of the clan's ancestry in their scales.
Homeland: the mainland of Assios, three generations back or one; in the islands, clan-houses in the Frontier ports and Goldwind.
Faith: clan ancestors, and whatever the clan swore to on the mainland.
Temperament: dutiful and precise. They find the islands' happy chaos alternately liberating and appalling.
Many strip their old imperial insignia and wear the bare stitch-marks proudly, which in any Frontier tavern is worth a bought drink.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A dragonborn veteran in Bastion still wears his imperial insignia, and the garrison has decided to let him.” (heard in Bastion)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: We cut the Emperor's badge off our coats. We kept the stitches, so we'd remember why.
epigraph.by: A dragonborn veteran in a Frontier tavern

illustration.alt: A bronze-scaled dragonborn veteran in a high-collared mainland coat accepts a drink in a snowy Frontier tavern, the bare stitch-marks where imperial insignia were removed plainly visible.
illustration.caption: We kept the stitches.

title: The Dwarves
subtitle: The folk of the Tally
summary: Hold and harbor crafters who enter every debt, favor, and grudge into an enduring ledger.

sections.title: The Tally
paragraphs: A promise is entered and does not lapse. A kindness to one generation may be repaid to another, with interest and a note. Dwarven craft is measured against everything the ancestors made.

sections.title: The Forge-Pantheon
paragraphs: The holds honor Durmakhâim the Quenching, Khazrûkk the Tally, and Varganthûr the Deep Hearth.

sections.title: Dress and courtesy
paragraphs: Heavy work-aprons cover fine mail. Hair and beard braids carry tally-beads recording obligations; inspecting a stranger’s beads without invitation is a serious insult. Hold-sigils appear at clasps and buckles.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Bromm, Durna, Khevik, Marga, Thraim, and Osgit; hold-names include Deephearth, Ironquill, Stonemark, and Emberdelf.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A dwarf's word, once given, is entered, and never lapses. The Tally is sacred because business is sacred, and so are old scores: a kindness done to a dwarf's grandmother will be repaid to her grandchild's creditor, with interest and a note.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about three and a half centuries.
Look: broad and strong, with beards and hair strung with tally-beads; each bead is a debt owed or owing.
Homeland: the deep holds of the mountain isles, where the dwarves are the unmatched finders and miners of Krysta, and the harbor-quarters of every great port.
Temperament: exact, loyal, and unforgiving of a broken word. A thing worth doing is worth doing so well it embarrasses the last person who did it.
Reading a stranger's tally-beads uninvited is grounds for a duel.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Cistern Door. At the bottom of Goldwind's oldest cistern is a dwarven wall, and someone has been working its mortar from the other side.” (common talk)
“Masons in seven dwarven holds have stopped talking about what they found on the shelf beside the wall.” (a dwarven mason's apprentice)
“The dwarves have an old word for the drow, and they will not say it in front of a banker.” (a Goldwind money-changer)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Never sleep on an open account.

illustration.alt: A dwarf teller closes an account by lamplight while a fellow craftsperson counts his own tally-beads, with a human customer behind them for scale.
illustration.caption: Every promise finds its place in the Tally.

title: The Elves
subtitle: Many branches of a long memory
summary: High, Wood, Sunwood, and Frost Elves live above the islands; the Ithrennai endure below.

sections.title: A shared inheritance
paragraphs: Elvenkind honors many-aspected Aelthuvar and remembers the Exodus from the Faewild through Castia. Shared memory has produced distinct peoples, each with its own place in the archipelago.

sections.title: High and Wood Elves
paragraphs: High Elves keep courtly, long-lived traditions; House Caelvaron’s Hundred-Year Throne is their great political expression. Severe silver-threaded dress can remain unchanged for a century. Names include Aellorien, Sylthaen, Caelia, and Ithral.
Wood Elves tend the temperate forests as practical wardens. Bark-dyed work layers and quiet hoods suit them better than finery. Fen, Lorel, Bryn, and Aske are familiar names.

sections.title: Sunwood and Frost Elves
paragraphs: Sunwood Elves are the dark-skinned elves of the southern jungles, long interwoven with native communities. Many mediate between chant-keepers and colonial law. Deep-colored robes, gold linings, warm tassels, jade, and a flower in the hair mark their dress; Isuel, Nayeth, Zorai, and Tamsel are common names.

Frost Elves live in the far southern ice. White furs, bone charms, and skull-paint serve as prayer and warning among those who emulate the White Hunger. Names include Ysgra, Khelvi, Drasna, and Hresk.

sections.title: The Ithrennai
paragraphs: The drow call themselves the Ithrennai, those who stayed. Surface accounts speak of ash-grey to slate skin, white hair, and faintly luminous eyes. Few surface elves discuss their kin Below. Travelers describe darksilk and light-veils, and names such as Ilvane, Oriandel, Iolith, and Sennarel.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about seven centuries. The High Elves of Caelvaron, who spend ten years in the Faewild for every hundred in the world, outlast even that. The drow, who give their light away, rarely see four.
Look and dress, by kind:
High Elves: severe, elegant lines, silver-threaded, a century out of fashion and entirely past caring.
Wood Elves: bark-dyed working layers and hoods, unornamented and silent.
Sunwood Elves: dark-skinned; layered deep-colored robes lined with gold, red and amber tassels, a single flower in the hair, jade and red stone.

Drow: tall and slender, skin from ash-grey to deep slate, hair white as cave-pearl, and eyes that hold a faint gold-white light of their own, which dims with age. Close-cut darksilk, hooded; abroad, a light-veil across the eyes. The surface, which almost never sees them, tells stories instead.
Faith: Aelthuvar, the many-aspected; the Frost Elves emulate the White Hunger, Vukharr.
Given names, by kind:
The drow keep no family names; a drow is known by the last of their line to give all at the Lamp.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Frost Elves have stopped raiding the Auroral Vault. The Frost Elves say Vukharr is dreaming of something new.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)
“Drow eyes. A drow's eyes shine in the dark, and the older the drow, the dimmer they shine.” (common talk)
“Hrothgar Icevein: he hunts the Frost Elves who exiled him.” (the docks, about the Most Wanted)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: We remember the founding arguments. We are still annoyed about them.
epigraph.by: A High Elf of House Caelvaron

illustration.alt: Two dark-skinned Sunwood Elves mediate a river-town agreement after rain, wearing gold-lined robes, jade, warm tassels and a flower in the chant-keeper’s hair.
illustration.caption: A patient word between two laws.

gallery.alt: Four adult surface Elves in a costume field guide: High in severe silver-threaded robes, Wood in bark-dyed work layers, Sunwood in gold-lined indigo and jade, and Frost in white furs and bone charms.
gallery.caption: Four branches of a long memory.
gallery.label: Elves of Kalvatar

title: The Gnomes
subtitle: The sparkfolk
summary: Tinkers, lens-grinders, and clockwrights who regard a closed mechanism as an invitation.

sections.title: The Tinkering Spark
paragraphs: Gnomes keep Tik, whose followers believe almost anything can be improved. The Council towns depend on their devices and know their workshops by the small fires as much as the clever inventions.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Many-pocketed vests, tool-bandoliers, bright caps, and magnifiers leave hands free to work. Soot is a respectable sign of effort.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Fizzet, Nimna, Wexle, Pemmi, and Quillo; workshop-names include Springloft, Copperquill, and Gearvale.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The gnomes' whole theology is that everything can be improved and most things should be opened first. They are endlessly curious, congenitally incapable of leaving a mechanism closed, and responsible, by their own cheerful accounting, for a quarter of the islands' clever devices and half of their small fires.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: around four centuries.
Look: small, quick, and bright-eyed, usually wearing a magnifier-monocle pushed up into a cap.
Homeland: the workshops of the Council towns, the lens-shops of Highspire, and (for the green-edge gnomes) the wilder fringes of the Heartland and the south.
Temperament: curious, inventive, and constitutionally unable to leave things alone.
Soot is considered proof of honest work.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A gnome workshop in Goldwind has built a clock that runs backward during the Still Days.” (heard in Goldwind)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Soot is proof of honest work. A clean gnome is either new or hiding something.

illustration.alt: Two adult gnome artisans work on lenses and a clock in a rainy Heartland workshop, wearing pocketed vests, bright caps, tool-bandoliers and magnifiers; an egg-sized brown rainfrog guards a satchel.
illustration.caption: It worked better before. Open it anyway.

title: The Goblinoids
subtitle: The Skarn’s children
summary: Warren-folk, salvage-tinkers, and sharp traders whose creed prizes survival over glory.

sections.title: The survivor-creed
paragraphs: Goblins, hobgoblins, and their kin honor the Skarn: the small and clever outlast the great and proud. They live around settlement edges and rough ports, often underestimated by the very people who depend on their work.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Mismatched finery and proud salvage record individual victories. Each piece has a story; a perfectly matched outfit is unusual enough to invite questions.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Skitt, Nakka, Grib, Motch, and Rezzi. Epithets are earned: Grib Twice-Sold, Nakka Underfoot.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Goblinoids are the warren-folk of the settlement edges and the rough ports: salvage-tinkers, sharp traders, and sharper survivors. They keep no thrones and hoard no glory, and they outlive everyone who does. Despised often, underestimated always, indispensable in the end.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: goblins about sixty years; hobgoblins and bugbears about eighty.
Look: goblins small and sharp-eared; hobgoblins upright and soldierly; bugbears tall, furred, and much quieter than they look.
Homeland: the warrens at the edge of every settlement, the salvage-yards, and the rough ports.
Temperament: practical, opportunistic, fiercely loyal to the warren, and allergic to anyone who looks down on them.
Dress: proud salvage, layered and mismatched, every piece a trophy with a story. A goblinoid in matching clothes is either grieving or up to something.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A goblin at the Knot is wearing a Council admiral's hat and has a very good story about it.” (heard at the Knot)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Every piece I wear, I won. Ask me about the hat. No, ask me about the hat.
epigraph.by: A goblin trader at the Knot

illustration.alt: A small goblin trader bargains with a soldierly hobgoblin and a human buyer at the Knot by candlelight, while a tall furred bugbear carries salvaged cloth through the shadows.
illustration.caption: Ask about the coat. Settle the price first.

title: The Goliaths
subtitle: A life measured in feats
summary: Stone-skinned high-range clanfolk who count every climb, carried weight, and achievement.

sections.title: Cousins in faith
paragraphs: Goliaths share high peaks, funerals, and guest-law with the Vorthani. They keep the rites of Vorthung alongside Khaurun’s, respecting the monks’ discipline while pursuing their own enduring competitions.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Furs and stone-bead sashes leave strong arms and shoulders exposed. The beads record feats and provide a visible measure of accomplishment.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Torug, Menhira, Karrak, Osska, and Dhurra. Deed-names follow: Karrak Seven-Peaks, Menhira Coldwater.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Where the Vorthani bank everything, the goliaths count everything: every climb, every carried weight, every feat is scored, bettered, and remembered. A goliath's life is one long friendly competition with everyone they have ever met, the dead included.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about ninety years.
Look: grey stone-patterned skin, often bald, arms and shoulders bared to the cold as discipline and scoreboard.

Ancestry in the islands: Storm's Thunder and Cloud's Jaunt are common on the high sea-cliffs; Frost's Chill in the far south; Stone's Endurance and Hill's Tumble in the Anvil Reach; Fire's Burn on the volcanic isles.
Temperament: competitive, cheerful, and fair. Cheating at a contest is the only real shame.
Dress: furs and stone-bead sashes; the beads are the tally of feats.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A goliath came down from the high ranges with a bead nobody has the right to wear: one for climbing the Sky Anvil.” (heard in the Anvil Reach)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Every bead is a mountain. Count them, then tell me I'm boasting.

illustration.alt: Two stone-skinned goliath climbers pause above the clouds of the Anvil Reach; a woman threads a new stone bead onto her feat-sash while a man coils the climbing rope, with a human companion for scale.
illustration.caption: One more bead. One more mountain.

title: The Half-Elves
subtitle: The bridge-folk
summary: Brokers, translators, captains, and go-betweens at home among the islands’ many overlapping cultures.

sections.title: At two tables
paragraphs: Half-elves are common wherever peoples meet. Many turn a mixed inheritance into a gift for negotiation, learning the habits and silences of more than one community.

sections.title: Dress and names
paragraphs: Chosen blends express which worlds a person claims: an elven line in an island cut, or house-colors worn in a southern style. Names may draw from either parent’s convention: Lorel Greycastle, Caelia Veyani, or Bryn Goldspire.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The ports are full of half-elven factors who can close a deal in four languages and a raised eyebrow, and many make a strength of the seam they were born on.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about a century and three quarters.
Look: a little of both parents, and in Kalvatar often a little of three or four peoples besides.
Homeland: every port, and above all the factors' quarters of Southhaven, Silverport, and Goldwind.
Faith: whatever their parents kept, or whatever pays.
Temperament: adaptable and watchful, billed by both tables and fluent in the silences of each.
Dress: deliberate blends, an elven line in an island cut, chosen as a statement about which worlds they claim.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A half-elf interpreter in Silverport has been offered a fortune to mistranslate a single word at a treaty table.” (heard in Silverport)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: I speak for both sides of the pier. That's why both sides pay me.

illustration.alt: Two half-elven port factors interpret between a northern captain and a Sunwood trader on a breezy Silverport quay, wearing deliberate blends of elven tailoring and island clothes.
illustration.caption: Both sides of the pier.

title: The Halflings
subtitle: The good quiet life
summary: Cooks, innkeepers, road-folk, and river-pilots who make settled Kalvatar feel like home.

sections.title: The well-laid table
paragraphs: Halflings keep Penny Greenstep, folk-saint of luck and hospitality. The common room is an excellent place to hear adventures; when trouble actually arrives, their practical steadiness is valued as highly as their cooking.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Comfortable waistcoats, walking cloaks, and reliable boots carry small luck-charms: a bent Bit, a river-stone, or a friend’s button.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Berrin, Posy, Tamlin, Wick, Marlow, and Etta. Kettleby, Thistledown, Hedgerow, and Greenstep are familiar hearth and hedge names.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Halflings hold that adventure is a thing that happens to other people, ideally within earshot of their common room. And yet no folk is steadier when the roof actually falls in, nor quicker back to the stew once it has been dealt with.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about a century and a half.
Homeland: the inns, teahouses, and river-ports of the Council towns; much of Southhaven's southleaf is halfling-grown.
Temperament: kind, unflappable, and deeply suspicious of anything that interrupts supper.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A halfling inn on the Heartland river roads has never once run out of beds, however many guests arrive.” (heard on the river roads)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Come in out of the rain. Dinner first, trouble after.

illustration.alt: Two adult halfling innkeepers in waistcoats and good boots welcome taller human travelers from the snow into a warm common room.
illustration.caption: Dinner first, trouble after.

title: The Humans
subtitle: The many rivers
summary: The islands’ most numerous people, shaped by northern descent, southern ancestry, and life at the cold edge.

sections.title: Three broad currents
paragraphs: The imperial-descended north keeps history in stone and charter, with formal houses, measured greetings, and the memory of the Exodus.
Ancestral southern communities keep spoken lineages, story-tattoos, and the law of the heart-fire. Their histories precede the Landing.
Whalers, hunters, and hold-folk of the far south keep memory in bone-carvings and law in the hold-lord’s hall.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Wool, iron, and house-colors belong to the north; capital fashion favors silk, sigils, and copper rings. Southern dress is flowing, gold-laden, and story-tattooed. The cold edge favors fur and carved bone.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Northern names include Aldric, Maren, Halvis, and Selen, with Greycastle or Goldspire. Southern names include Jaseh, Lumai, Tiagu, and Ayanu, with Veyani or Okonja. The cold edge uses Halvar, Astri, Bjarn, and Senna, with Frostmark or Kaldsen.

sections.title: The three currents
paragraphs: Each current suggests a skill for Skillful and an Origin feat for Versatile, though any choice is open.
The imperial-descended north (the Frontier and the Heartland): ordered, formal, name-and-house folk who keep their history in stone and charter. Try History or Persuasion, and Alert or Flag-Sworn.
Try Survival, Medicine, or Performance, and The Spoken Line or Magic Initiate.
Try Athletics or Survival, and Tough or Keeper of the Fire.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about eighty years.
Faith: the Concord in Council lands; Yaxqel and the chant-keepers' ways in the native south; the Aspects, raw and old, on the ice.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Jakupur trader and a Frontier lord were seen drinking together in Goldwind, laughing. Both deny it.” (heard in Goldwind)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: The north gave us iron, the south gave us gold, the ice gave us patience. The sea gave us each other.

illustration.alt: Four humans from the Frontier, Heartland, ancestral south and cold edge move a laden cart together during a summer squall in Goldwind.
illustration.caption: The sea gave us each other.

title: The Kobolds
subtitle: The Underscale’s own
summary: Small, communal scale-folk who make a living in warrens, mines, and the tight spaces beneath the docks.

sections.title: The warren keeps it
paragraphs: Kobolds honor Vrix the Underscale and claim distant kinship with true dragons. Individuals own little; the warren owns much, and useful material is never thrown away. Their engineers and trap-makers excel where larger workers cannot fit.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Tool-harnesses and scavenged scale do double duty as equipment and adornment. Wealth hangs where the whole warren can admire it.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Tikka, Skex, Mizzit, Krik, and Zazz. The shared warren serves as a family name: Zazz of the Third Under.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Kobolds are the survivors of warren, mine, and underdock. They are industrious and fiercely communal: a kobold owns little, the warren owns much, and nothing is ever thrown away. They are the best small-space engineers coin can hire, provided coin is polite about it.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about a century, if the warren is lucky.
Look: about three feet tall, Small at the shorter end of that size, scaled and quick, with a crest or frill in the warren's color.
Homeland: the warrens under mines and docks, and the upper galleries Below that the dwarves walled off and the kobolds quietly use.
Temperament: busy, communal, practical, and very hard to offend, except by waste.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A kobold warren under Duskmire has started selling maps of the tunnels below. Every map is a little different.” (heard at the Knot)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Small hands, small tunnels, big ideas.

illustration.alt: Three small kobold engineers in tool-harnesses raise a supply crate through a narrow warren using a simple rope hoist; their shared jade crests mark the warren.
illustration.caption: Nothing wasted. Everyone paid.

title: The Lizardfolk
subtitle: The cold-blooded pragmatists
summary: Patient folk of swamp and shore who take bargains at their exact words.

sections.title: A deliberate people
paragraphs: Lizardfolk waste little, plan far ahead, and study the warm-blooded habit of speaking without meaning what was said. The bog-tribes honor Sszathra, the Cold-Blooded Mother, alongside Ssvayuk, whom some call her living hand.

sections.title: Dress and status
paragraphs: Harnesses, belts, shell, bone, and mud-paint serve as equipment, dress, rank, and prayer. An overnight change of paint can mark an important change of standing.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Sszara, Hessk, Yssith, Karssh, and Ozzek; tribe-names refer to water: Hessk of the Slow Water.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Lizardfolk are patient, literal, and unsentimental. They waste nothing, mourn briefly, plan long, and find the warm-blooded habit of saying things they don't mean a source of endless quiet study.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about seventy years.
Look: scaled and long-jawed, with mud-paint laid in patterns that serve as clothing, rank, and prayer at once.
Homeland: the swamps and shores of the Southern Wilds; the bog-tribes.
Temperament: literal and loyal to the letter. A lizardfolk repainted overnight has changed status, and it is wise to notice.

sections.title: Playing one of the lizardfolk
paragraphs: Why you are among the warm-blooded: a bargain sent you; the tribe needs something only the colonies have; or you are studying them, and they are fascinating.
Classes that fit: druid, barbarian, ranger, monk.
Backgrounds that fit: Saurian Handler, Grove Warden, Pearl Diver.
Heritage feat: Clamping Jaws.
Hooks: a contract whose exact words you intend to keep; what the mud said about a member of your party; the Savage Lord's progeny moving in the bog.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A lizardfolk elder repainted herself in a pattern no one has worn in a hundred years.” (heard in the great bogs)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: I was repainted at dawn. Look closer, and speak more carefully.
epigraph.by: A lizardfolk elder of the Slow Water

illustration.alt: Two powerful, muscular lizardfolk hunters with stone and bone weapons, heavy tails and rugged hide equipment in a mangrove forest.
illustration.caption: Look closer. Speak carefully.

title: The Marked
subtitle: A door held open
summary: Tieflings and aasimar, whose visible inheritances have fostered a culture of discretion and mutual aid.

sections.title: The people of the pact
paragraphs: The daemon-touched wear horns; the celestial-touched carry light. Unfair suspicion has made wit, advocacy, and dependable mutual aid central to Marked communities. Under Nethis, lord of pacts, a Marked door is open to a Marked stranger and a debt is honored.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Gloves, high collars, horn-caps, and veils can conceal or celebrate an inheritance. The wearer chooses, and both choices are respected.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Family names such as Nemis, Orith, Sarran, and Liorel are kept close. Many also take a chosen name held as a vow: Mercy, Ledger, Hale, or Even.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A Marked door is never closed to a Marked stranger, and a debt among the Marked is paid.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: a little longer than humans.
Temperament: a people the world watches learns early to be twice as good and half as loud. The isles' finest brokers, advocates, and fixers are disproportionately horned, glowing, or both.

sections.title: Playing one of the Marked
paragraphs: Why you are here: you owe a Marked debt, or are owed one; a house wants a fixer it can disown; or your light or your horns finally made a choice for you.
Classes that fit: warlock, sorcerer, paladin, bard.
Backgrounds that fit: Factor, Undertow Runner, Registry Scholar.
Heritage feat: The Chosen Name.
Hooks: the pact in your blood and who still holds the other half; House Alastor's interest in you; a Marked door you were turned away from, which should never happen.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “One crate of Darlath stone in twelve leaves Everfall marked 'broken' and is never seen at the refinery.” (an Everfall carter)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Some of us hide our horns. Some of us crown them. Both are choices, and both are ours.
epigraph.by: One of the Marked, at a Goldwind salon

illustration.alt: A veiled tiefling advocate welcomes an aasimar traveler into a Heartland salon while a second tiefling proudly wears simple horn-caps, showing different choices of how to carry an inheritance.
illustration.caption: Come in. A debt can wait until morning.

title: The Orcs & Half-Orcs
subtitle: Heirs of the fallen Orka
summary: Descendants of an ancient empire who preserve their family histories through the Telling.

sections.title: What to carry forward
paragraphs: Coastal and jungle clans keep the Tusk-Marking and recite family lines back toward the Orka’s fall. Gorrokar’s present war-rites are lean and private, deliberately distant from the empire’s excesses. In the ports, many work as drovers, dockhands, guards, and Hunters.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Drover leather, sailor’s canvas, tusk-rings, and lineage tattoos are familiar. Old imperial glyphs are worn carefully, after the full Telling has been earned.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Karguz, Morgha, Uzzek, Hargra, and Dresha. The Telling grants deed-names such as Morgha Wall-Holder or Uzzek Rope-and-Knife.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The orcs descend from the Orka, whose daemon-bought empire drowned in the age called the Wonder, and they have spent every generation since deciding what of it to carry and what to leave in the water. Through the Telling, every family's spoken line runs back toward the fall, so that no orc is ever without a history and no history is ever without a warning.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about eighty years.
Homeland: the tribes of coast and jungle, and the rough trades of every port: dockhands, drovers, guards, and Hunters. The Longshore's Goldwind boss, Morgha Wall-Holder, is an orc.
Faith: Gorrokar's war-rites, kept lean and private, nothing like the old empire's excess, which is rather the point.
Temperament: direct, loyal, and wary of anything that smells of the old empire's bargains.
Dress: drover leathers and sailor's canvas, tusk-rings, and the Tusk-Marking.
Half-orcs use the Orc traits or the Human traits, and keep the Telling if their family does.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “An orc chieftain in the south is said to have buried a daemon-mask at sea, on purpose, with a Telling sung over it.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Our grandfathers' grandfathers wore the masks. We wear the Telling instead.
epigraph.by: An orc elder at a Telling

illustration.alt: An orc elder engraves a young adult orc's lower tusk during the Telling, while an adult half-orc woman listens beside a small fire under the southern trees.
illustration.caption: A history to carry forward.

title: The Anvil Reach
subtitle: Where the jungle surrenders to stone
summary: The cold cordillera of the Southern Wilds, homeland of the Vorthani and their high monasteries.

sections.title: The Ascents
paragraphs: The jungle climbs into stone and permanent snow. Above the cloudline stand the Ascents, named by their order of founding. The First Ascent crowns the Sky Anvil, where Vorthani say the air is thin enough to hear Khaurun think.

sections.title: Keepers of the sky-records
paragraphs: From the Reach, generations record the battles of Kayuntu and Badron across the five skies. The records serve as omen and calendar, and the Aethyn exchange star-charts for them.

sections.title: Mountain law
paragraphs: The Reach signs no charter and turns away no honest guest. Arrivals receive warmth, broth, and a bed; before leaving, each carries a stone.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: The road climbs out of the jungle into stone, then into snow. A traveler who reaches an Ascent is given broth, a bed, and silence, with questions held until morning. The thin air at the Sky Anvil makes lowlanders dizzy; the monks say that is the point.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Anvil Reach is the homeland of the Vorthani, the four-armed monastery giants, and the Ascents are their monasteries, each named in the order of its founding. The price is labor: every guest carries one stone somewhere before they leave. Half the walls of the First Ascent, the monks note serenely, were carried by strangers.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Vorthani First Ascent has taken in a guest who will not carry a stone. The monks say she is not a guest.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: You will be tired at the top. That is the first lesson.
epigraph.by: A Vorthani teacher to a lowland guest

illustration.alt: A four-armed Vorthani receives a traveler carrying a stone to a monastery above the jungle and clouds.
illustration.caption: A guest carries a stone before leaving an Ascent.

title: The Widow’s Teeth
subtitle: Lamps above the singing fog
summary: A fang-row of sea-stacks off Greyhaven, threaded by the Gap of Sorrows.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Fog sings among the stacks. Ships pass a cliff-shrine lit by widows’ lamps as they thread the Gap of Sorrows.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Ships out of Greyhaven thread the Gap of Sorrows by lamplight, with a pilot and a prayer. On the cliff-shrine above, the widows keep their lamps lit for the men the Teeth took, and a captain who passes without dipping his own light once is not welcome back in Greyhaven.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: On still nights the wind moves through the holes in the rock and makes a chord that the Greyhaven folk take for the voices of the drowned. Harbor-masters read the next day's weather by the pitch of the Teeth, and some of them swear the chord has changed in the last ten years.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Widow's Teeth are singing a new tune. The old women say a boat will be lost in the Gap before the Murk is over.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)

epigraph.quote: Dip your light for the widows, or the Teeth will dip it for you.

illustration.alt: A Greyhaven pilot dips a lantern while threading the Gap of Sorrows beneath the Widow’s Teeth.
illustration.caption: The widows’ lamps remain lit above the Gap.

title: The Soldiers’ Rest
subtitle: A truce in the water
summary: Terraced mineral hot springs near Bastion, protected by an iron custom of peace.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: No steel is drawn at the springs. Even a blood-feud pauses while its enemies share the water.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Terraced pools steam on the hillside near Bastion, and the water tastes of iron and salt. Anyone may bathe; no one may draw steel. Old enemies have been seen sharing a pool in silence and leaving by different roads.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Someone drew steel at the Soldiers' Rest last winter. The springs ran cold for a week.” (heard in Bastion)

epigraph.quote: I sat in the water across from the man who killed my brother. We said nothing. Then we both went home.

illustration.alt: Two old adversaries rest in terraced mineral springs near Bastion while their weapons remain sheathed.
illustration.caption: No steel is drawn at the Soldiers’ Rest.

title: Malim’s Stair
subtitle: The Laughing Flood
summary: A mile of river terraces and falls, sacred to the Laughing Flood.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: The Laughing Water festival gathers at the foot of the Stair. Swimming its course is among the south’s most famous dares.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: A mile of river terraces and falls drops in white steps toward the coast. At the Laughing Water the river tribes gather at its foot with fruit and music for Malim, and the boldest swim the Stair from top to bottom. Most are fished out halfway.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Malim's worshippers say the river is a child who must be entertained, and the Stair has broken more than one bold swimmer's bones.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A swimmer reached the bottom of Malim's Stair laughing, without a scratch, and swore the river had carried her the whole way.” (heard at the Laughing Water)

epigraph.quote: Malim is a child who must be entertained. So we sing, and we bring fruit, and the fools swim.
epigraph.by: A river priestess at the Laughing Water

illustration.alt: The Laughing Water festival gathers with fruit and music below the long cascade of Malim’s Stair.
illustration.caption: The river tribes gather at the foot of the Stair.

title: The Bonewilds
subtitle: Shakarr’s country
summary: White flats strewn with the sun-bleached bones of titans.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Nothing scavenges the half-buried bones. Islanders call the flats Shakarr’s country and approach accordingly.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: The white flats lie under a pitiless sun, and some of the bones in them are bigger than ships. No one crosses after dusk. Guides walk the edge in silence and never point at anything.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The jackals and the carrion-birds do not enter, and the Shakarr of the Bonewilds is said to walk the flats at dusk, counting the dead.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A guide says one of the bones on the white flats has moved, a little, every year since he was a boy.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

epigraph.quote: Don't point. Don't run. And don't count the bones out loud.
epigraph.by: A native guide at the edge of the flats

illustration.alt: Travelers pause at the edge of the Bonewilds among the sun-bleached bones of titans.
illustration.caption: No one crosses after dusk.

title: The Mirrormere
subtitle: Two moons, doubled
summary: A crater lake whose extraordinary stillness mirrors both moons.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Chant-keepers read omens in the doubled sky. Touching the water at moonrise is taboo.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: On a clear night both moons float in the crater lake, perfect and still. Chant-keepers come to read the doubled sky. At moonrise, no hand touches the water.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Those who break the taboo are said to see the reflection of the moon move on its own, and then to see their own faces in it, aged by a lifetime in a single breath.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “On the last night of the King Tide, a third moon was seen in the Mirrormere.” (heard among the chant-keepers)

epigraph.quote: Two moons above, two moons below. Touch the water and the lower ones are yours forever.

illustration.alt: A chant-keeper studies both moons reflected without ripples in the Mirrormere.
illustration.caption: At moonrise, no hand touches the water.

title: The Whalefall Gardens
subtitle: Life beneath the leviathans
summary: A shallow bay where fallen leviathans seed gardens of pale life.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Whalers hold the bay sacred. The Grey Fathoms are said to watch the gardens.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: When a great whale dies and sinks into the shallow bay, a garden of pale life grows from it: white fronds, glass-clear shrimp, and fish no one has named. Whalers neither hunt nor fish in the bay, and they come here to remember the boats they lost.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Something pale has been walking the bottom of the Whalefall Gardens at low water, tending them.” (heard in Frosthold)

epigraph.quote: When a whale falls, the sea plants a garden. We come here to remember the boats that fell with them.

illustration.alt: Pale fronds and small sea creatures grow around a fallen whale on the floor of an icy shallow bay.
illustration.caption: A fallen leviathan feeds a garden of pale life.

title: The Stillwater
subtitle: Where no wind crosses
summary: A becalmed circle in the open sea where compasses spin.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: The Old Shells surface here. Sailors claim the Still Days take their name from this water; their story is a harbor telling rather than a chartwright’s certainty.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: A circle of glassy sea that no wind crosses, even in a storm. A sailing ship that drifts in must be rowed or towed out. The Old Shells, the great sage-turtles, surface here, and a crew that sees one keeps its distance and its voice low.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Compasses spin in it, and the sea is glassy in every storm.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Stillwater has moved three leagues west. The Armada's charts say it has always been there. The sailors say it has always been moving.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“The Old Shells have surfaced at the Stillwater three times this year. They used to come up once in a generation.” (a Last Psalm Tidecaller)

epigraph.quote: No wind, no current, and the compass spinning like a top. Row, lads, and don't look down.

title: The Drowned Colonnade
subtitle: Pillars at low water
summary: Orka-era pillars that emerge from the open sea at low tide.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Charts mark them, but captains do not linger. At King Tide the Hollow Song is said to echo up the stone.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: At low tide a line of carved pillars rises out of the open sea, crusted with shell. Every chart marks it, every captain gives it a wide berth, and nobody fishes in its shadow.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Emri has been seen swimming past the Drowned Colonnade with a bundle of silver on her back. Nobody has asked her what she is carrying.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

epigraph.quote: Mark it on the chart, give it a mile, and don't fish in its shadow. My grandfather did, once.

illustration.alt: Carved Orka columns rise from the sea at low tide while a distant sail keeps clear.
illustration.caption: Captains chart the Colonnade and leave it alone.

title: The Keeping
subtitle: The keeper eats last
summary: The quiet hearth rite of lighting the fire and beginning the food for those who come after.

sections.title: Before the others wake
paragraphs: Someone rises alone in the dark, lights the fire, and starts the slow food. The act is not announced. The keeper eats last, standing; it is the humblest rite of the Hunger That Warms.

sections.title: Passing the irons
paragraphs: Held out wordlessly, the fire-irons pass care and belonging to the next keeper. A newcomer with no one to feed lights the fire anyway. People come because the fire is lit.

sections.title: Someone small at the hearth
paragraphs: The hearth newt sleeps on the first coal and keeps it alive until dawn. When the irons pass to a new keeper, the newt usually follows.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The passing of the irons: when a keeper silently hands someone the fire-irons, the tongs and the poker, that person has been adopted into the household: you are mine now, and the mornings are yours.
"Someone kept the fire on that one" means quiet, unthanked work.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “In one Frontier village the fire was lit every morning for a year after the last keeper died, and nobody ever saw who lit it.” (heard on the Frontier)

source: Bible Lite · §10; Beasts and Companions · p. 7

epigraph.quote: The keeper eats last, standing, and says nothing about it. That's how you know it's love.

title: Hearth and Harbor Customs
subtitle: We still have salt between us
summary: The small gestures by which islanders welcome strangers, remember sailors, and become family.

sections.title: A place kept ready
paragraphs: The Returning Cup hangs upside down for an absent sailor; it is turned upright in the window when a return is due. Neighbors leave food. Coastal homes dip an Answering Light once for a passing ship.

sections.title: The street cares for its own
paragraphs: After a storm, the Mending begins with the worst roof. First Bread is a newcomer’s meal secretly paid for by a stranger. Surplus on the windowsill is free to take: the Sill provides.

sections.title: Growing up and coming home
paragraphs: A child’s Naming Spoon hangs on the kitchen wall. Taking it down means leaving home; hanging it again means returning. The first companion’s name is carved on the reverse.

sections.title: Promises that endure
paragraphs: Winter-kin have shared a winter and are owed a plate and bed for life. A Salt Promise divides two pinches from one cellar, to be cooked together when the friends reunite. Promise doves are given to keep such a bond visible.

sections.title: The harbor’s little records
paragraphs: Children chalk high water on the harbor steps. First-year visitors leave a Bit on a house’s lintel; a full row of Door Coins declares the house paid true.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Returning Cup in Easthold turned itself upright in the window, and the sailor it waited for walked in the next morning.” (heard in Easthold)

source: Bible Lite · §10; Beasts and Companions · Part One

epigraph.quote: The cup in the window is upside down until he's due. Then I turn it, and I wait.

title: Kellum
subtitle: Salt and kin!
summary: The honeywrack-kelp spirit distilled in every port, tasting of its own sea.

sections.title: The first drop
paragraphs: The first drop goes over the rail. The Armada’s daily serving is the Charter’s tot. “Salt and kin!” is answered with “Fair tide home!”

sections.title: The water behind the cup
paragraphs: Stillwright herds of wrack cows graze the honeywrack beds and tow the harbor’s barges. A harbor with wrack cows is a harbor that distills kellum.

sections.title: The four great styles
paragraphs: Greywater (Northern Frontier): clear, cold, and peppery, drunk from a tin cup in a single swallow. *Sipping greywater is how you tell a Heartlander.*
Burnmouth (Southern Wilds): dark kellum steeped with cacao husk, fire-pepper, and cane-sugar until it bites back. Southerners drink it with fruit; northerners drink it once.
Icebrand (Icy Expanse): left out in the killing cold, the ice pulled off it again and again, then smoked over whale-oil fires. It is said to be the only thing that can make a Frost Elf smile.

sections.title: The customs of kellum
paragraphs: Because honeywrack grows in every water, every harbor has its stillhouse and every stillhouse its rivals, and each kellum tastes of its own sea. Aboard ship the first drop of any bottle goes over the rail, and the Armada pours a quarter-cup at the noon bell: the Charter's tot.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Goldwind stillhouse has a cask of Icebrand old enough to have come off the first whaling ships. It is not for sale, which is why everyone wants it.” (heard in Goldwind)

source: Bible Lite · §8; Beasts and Companions · pp. 29–30

epigraph.quote: Salt and kin!
epigraph.by: A toast, answered with: Fair tide home!

title: Brightleaf
subtitle: The hot cup
summary: The tea of Sunhold’s terraces, carried throughout the islands in pressed bricks.

sections.title: A cup by region
paragraphs: The Frontier takes hold-tea with butter and salt. Heartland cups are pale with citrus. Southern pepperleaf competes with Southhaven coffee. In the ice, fat-tea warms the long dark.

sections.title: The terraces
paragraphs: Sunhold’s growers send terrace ducks through the plants to eat leaf-beetles. The dawn duck parade is famous almost as widely as the tea itself. Pressed leaf-bricks can pass as money at sea.

sections.title: The courteous moth
paragraphs: Teahouses prize a teacup moth to keep a full cup warm. Sweet brightleaf left on a sill may win one’s company.

sections.title: Everyone drinks it; no two regions agree how
paragraphs: Hold-tea (Northern Frontier): brewed black and bitter, churned with butter and a pinch of salt. Thick enough, they say, to caulk a hull.
Fat-tea (Icy Expanse): churned with rendered seal fat and salt. Visitors find it horrifying, and regret mocking it by the third day.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The coffee-houses of Goldwind fight the terrace-growers over it with the fervor of a feud.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Scarlet Mother's priest was seen in Southhaven buying the Fennick factors' coffee in bulk. Nobody says what he wants with so much of it.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“The Sunhold terraces grow a brightleaf that the Registry buys every leaf of, and nobody has ever been allowed to taste it.” (a Terrace Guild picker)

facts: Pressed bricks may serve as barter
source: Bible Lite · §8; Beasts and Companions · pp. 6–7, 31–32

epigraph.quote: Hold-tea should be thick enough to caulk a hull. Anything thinner is a rumor of tea.

title: Swordtooth
subtitle: Azarox · War tradition
summary: A lean, fierce predator and the classic cavalry mount of Jakupur.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Fast, mid-sized, and just trainable enough to ride into battle, the Swordtooth is the backbone of southern saurian cavalry.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Its Common name describes its prominent, bladelike fangs. Azarox is the older Kalvatari name used by southern handlers.

sections.title: In the stables and the wild
paragraphs: The classic war-mount of Jakupur: a lean, fierce mid-sized predator, fast and vicious and just trainable enough to ride into battle. The backbone of saurian cavalry and the iconic image of southern strength.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: Jakupur's war-mount and the backbone of saurian cavalry. A trained one costs 100 to 300 Anchors, double under the Sukuun mark. A wild pack is a death sentence.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A wild swordtooth pack has learned to wait outside Jakupur's gates at the hour the caravans leave.” (heard in Jakupur)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Swordtooth: Azarox
illustration.alt: A lean Swordtooth waits beside its adult rider in a shaded Jakupur training court.
illustration.caption: A lean Swordtooth waits beside its adult rider in a shaded Jakupur training court.

epigraph.quote: A Swordtooth will die for you. It will also bite you on Tuesdays.

gallery.alt: Saurian riders and fruit sellers move through Jakupur’s wet stepped streets above a jungle river.
gallery.caption: After rain, the White Flame watches the streets steam.
gallery.label: Saurians at work in Jakupur

title: Dreadmaw
subtitle: Tzharrok · War tradition
summary: A towering predatory siege-beast, rare, dangerous, and ruinously expensive.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: A trained Dreadmaw can break a battle-line. Its immense size and dangerous temper make it a formidable responsibility even for the keepers of Jakupur.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Tana Sukuun is famed for her bond with Old Thunder, a rose-grey Dreadmaw. A keeper reads the beast through a lifelong relationship, rather than treating it as an ordinary mount.

sections.title: In the stables and the wild
paragraphs: The apex war-beast: a towering predator, a walking siege-engine descended (in the deepest sense) from Tyrak'Zhul himself. Rare, ruinously expensive, and dangerous to its own keepers; a single trained Tzharrok can break a battle-line.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Dreadmaw: Tzharrok
illustration.alt: A towering rose-grey Dreadmaw dwarfs an adult keeper at the Sukuun stables.
illustration.caption: A towering rose-grey Dreadmaw dwarfs an adult keeper at the Sukuun stables.

epigraph.quote: You don't own a Dreadmaw. You negotiate with it, every day, and you hope.

title: Thornback
subtitle: Korzak · War tradition
summary: A low, immensely armored guardian: a living wall of bony plates and spikes.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Thornbacks serve as mobile walls, battering rams, and guardians. Their dense armor is their defining strength.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: The Common name pairs a sharp feature with the armored back. Southern handlers also call the beast Korzak.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The living fortress: a mobile wall, a battering ram, a guardian. Its shed plates are worked into armor in Jakupur.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Jakupur noble walled his garden with live thornbacks instead of stone. His neighbors sleep badly.” (heard in Jakupur)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Thornback: Korzak
illustration.alt: An armored Thornback rests beside an adult gatekeeper at a southern city gate.
illustration.caption: An armored Thornback rests beside an adult gatekeeper at a southern city gate.

epigraph.quote: Stand behind the Thornback and the arrows go somewhere else.

title: Lashtail
subtitle: Tzulak · War tradition
summary: A long-bodied saurian whose powerful weapon-tail can shatter shields.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Temperamental and dangerous in trained hands, the Lashtail can sweep a rank off its feet with a blow of its tail.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Its Common name identifies its whiplike attack. Tzulak is the name used in Kalvatari.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The whip-tail of Jakupur's fighting pits. Temperamental, and a terror in trained hands.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A lashtail in the Maw-Pit broke three shields in one bout and then refused to fight anyone without one.” (heard at the Maw-Pit)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Lashtail: Tzulak
illustration.alt: A handler gives a Lashtail room to turn its long weapon-tail in a sandy practice enclosure.
illustration.caption: A handler gives a Lashtail room to turn its long weapon-tail in a sandy practice enclosure.

epigraph.quote: Watch the tail, not the teeth. The teeth are a distraction.

title: Swiftcrest
subtitle: Sissix · Speed tradition
summary: A tall, slender, crested racing saurian built for speed and swift scouting.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Long-legged and beautiful, the Swiftcrest is the premier racing saurian of the south and a favored fast scout-mount.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: The Sunspine Run stands on Jakupur’s edge. Its famous silver-crested champion, Sissix-the-Comet, is known throughout the racing circuit.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The racer of the Great Track, and a couriers' and outriders' mount. From 150 Anchors for a plodder to 5,000 for a champion's bloodline.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Sissix-the-Comet has lost a heat for the first time in two seasons. The jockey who beat her has a Vossreth brand on his wrist and no memory of the race.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Swiftcrest: Sissix
illustration.alt: A silver-crested Swiftcrest and adult jockey wait at the Sunspine Run.
illustration.caption: A silver-crested Swiftcrest and adult jockey wait at the Sunspine Run.

epigraph.quote: A plodder costs a hundred and fifty Anchors. A champion costs your house.

title: Glidetalon
subtitle: Vollun · Sky tradition
summary: A light, feathered saurian that glides and bounds over rough terrain.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Quick and clever, the Glidetalon carries scouts and messages across difficult ground through gliding and bounding movement.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: It belongs to the southern traditions of speed and sky. Vollun is its Kalvatari name.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The scout of the air, carrying Small scouts and messages over rough country. Wild ones hunt in murders like winged jackals.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A glidetalon carried a scout's message forty miles over the jungle in a single afternoon, and the scout has never been found.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Glidetalon: Vollun
illustration.alt: A feathered Glidetalon launches from a forest platform carrying a small message case.
illustration.caption: A feathered Glidetalon launches from a forest platform carrying a small message case.

epigraph.quote: Small rider, light pack, long glide. Don't eat breakfast.

title: Skyfin
subtitle: Aetzox · Sky tradition
summary: A large leather-winged saurian capable of sustained flight, prized as an aerial mount.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Rare and coveted, the Skyfin can maintain flight rather than merely gliding. It is one of the south’s most sought-after mounts.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Aetzox is the older Kalvatari name. Its flight belongs to the living wealth of the Southern Wilds.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The true flyer of the south, nesting on high cliffs; the rare and coveted aerial mount. Its membrane is hunted for the rarest of constructions.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Skyfin rider claims she flew high enough to see the whole south at once, and that something was looking back.” (heard in Jakupur)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Skyfin: Aetzox
illustration.alt: A giant long-beaked Skyfin opens its enormous membrane wings beside an adult barefoot rider on a coastal terrace.
illustration.caption: A Skyfin opens its leather wings beside an adult rider on a coastal launch terrace.

epigraph.quote: From the back of a Skyfin the whole south looks like a promise.

title: Loamback
subtitle: Mokun · Labor tradition
summary: A massive, placid, long-necked hauler: the south’s plough-beast and freight-carrier.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Loambacks pull, carry freight, and help build the cities of the south. Jakupur was built on Mokun labor.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: A quiet working investment, the Mokun is tended through generations of southern handling. Its strength serves fields, freight roads, and construction sites.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The great hauler, the south's plough-beast and construction-engine; Jakupur was built on its labor. About 100 Anchors trained to harness.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The oldest loamback in Jakupur's quarries will only haul stone for one family, and that family is three generations dead.” (heard in Jakupur)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Loamback: Mokun
illustration.alt: A placid long-necked Loamback hauls a timber cart beside adult workers.
illustration.caption: A placid long-necked Loamback hauls a timber cart beside adult workers.

epigraph.quote: Jakupur wasn't built by kings. It was built by Loambacks.

gallery.alt: Saurian riders and fruit sellers move through Jakupur’s wet stepped streets above a jungle river.
gallery.caption: After rain, the White Flame watches the streets steam.
gallery.label: Saurians at work in Jakupur

title: Altisaur
subtitle: Yaltox · Labor tradition
summary: The tallest domesticated saurian, a towering long-necked hauler and living platform.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Altisaurs raise great structures, carry the heaviest loads, and serve as living platforms. Their extraordinary height sets them apart from the other domesticated kinds.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Yaltox is the Kalvatari name. This great working beast is a small mountain in the service of southern builders.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “An altisaur carried a wedding party across a flooded river without spilling a single cup.” (heard on the Jakupur road)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Altisaur: Yaltox
illustration.alt: An Altisaur towers above adult builders and a multi-storey construction site.
illustration.caption: An Altisaur towers above adult builders and a multi-storey construction site.

epigraph.quote: A small mountain that works for you, and eats like three.

title: Craghorn
subtitle: Gormak · Labor tradition
summary: A sturdy horned-and-frilled worker, strong, stubborn, and ready to defend itself.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Craghorns haul and plough. An approaching predator must also reckon with their horns and ill-tempered strength.

A craghorn puts its strength to work close to the ground, pulling a plough through soil or hauling a load behind it. That same build makes it formidable when threatened: the horns that a farmer works beside every day can make a predator reconsider its approach.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Gormak is the Kalvatari name for this southern working saurian.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A craghorn gored a tax collector in a southern village and the magistrate ruled it self-defense.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Craghorn: Gormak
illustration.alt: A sturdy Craghorn pulls a plough while an adult farmer walks beside it.
illustration.caption: A sturdy Craghorn pulls a plough while an adult farmer walks beside it.

epigraph.quote: Strong as an ox, stubborn as two, and it remembers who shouted at it.

title: Murkstrider
subtitle: Marrox · Water tradition
summary: A long-legged fish-eating wader, ridden through swamp paths and shallows.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Murkstriders cross the marsh paths where other mounts struggle. Their long legs and comfort in the shallows make them the mounts of the bog-tribes.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Marrox is the Kalvatari name for this fish-eating saurian of the Southern Wilds.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A murkstrider walked a lost child home through the bog and would not leave until it was fed.” (heard among the bog-tribes)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Murkstrider: Marrox
illustration.alt: A long-legged Murkstrider carries an adult traveler along a shallow marsh path.
illustration.caption: A long-legged Murkstrider carries an adult traveler along a shallow marsh path.

epigraph.quote: Where a horse sinks, a Murkstrider strolls.

title: Mirewallow
subtitle: Sszuka · Water tradition
summary: A heavy semi-aquatic bog-beast, sluggish on land and formidable in water.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: A Mirewallow lives between mud and water. Its slow landward movement gives little warning of how dangerous it can be once afloat.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Southern marsh people know the beast as Sszuka. Its home is the wetlands of the Southern Wilds.

sections.title: In the stables and the wild
paragraphs: The bog-beast: a heavy, semi-aquatic, mud-dweller, kin (the lizardfolk say) to the Savage Lord Ssvayuk himself. Sluggish on land, terrifying in the water.

sections.title: What the handlers say
paragraphs: The bog-beast, kin (the lizardfolk say) to Ssvayuk. Harmless unless startled, then catastrophic.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A trader camped for a week on an island in the delta. On the eighth morning the island left.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Mirewallow: Sszuka
illustration.alt: A heavy Mirewallow rests at a muddy riverbank with an adult observer on a raised walkway.
illustration.caption: A heavy Mirewallow rests at a muddy riverbank with an adult observer on a raised walkway.

epigraph.quote: Harmless, until you startle it. Then you are part of the bog.

title: Razorfin
subtitle: Razku · Water tradition
summary: A sleek finned predator of rivers and coasts, rarely tamed and never trusted.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Razorfin is known for jaws and speed. Its aquatic hunting grounds reach from southern rivers to the coast.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: The Kalvatari name is Razku. Even a rarely trained animal does not become a trusted household beast.

sections.title: In the stables and the wild
paragraphs: The river-killer: a sleek, finned, aquatic predator of rivers and coasts, all jaws and speed. Rarely tamed and never trusted.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The razorfins of one river have stopped taking the bait, and the boatmen say they are waiting for something bigger.” (heard on the Murkstrider routes)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Razorfin: Razku
illustration.alt: A wild Razorfin moves beneath clear coastal river water, seen beside a distant human canoe.
illustration.caption: A wild Razorfin moves beneath clear coastal river water, seen beside a distant human canoe.

epigraph.quote: Count the fins in the river before you count the fish.

title: Bellowback
subtitle: Bumako · Table tradition
summary: A big, placid herd-grazer raised for meat, hide, and great clutches of eggs.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Bellowbacks graze the savannas and jungle edges in large herds. Their deep lowing call gives them their Common name.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Bumako husbandry is a foundation of southern food and farming. Gentle and slow, they are among the first beasts a southern child learns to mind. Like all saurians, they lay eggs and give no milk.

sections.title: In the stables and the wild
paragraphs: The cattle of the south: a big, placid, broad-bodied herd-grazer with a deep, lowing bellow, raised across the savannas and jungle-edges for meat, hide, and great clutches of eggs. After the fowl, the Bumako is the single most important food-saurian alive, the beef of Kalvatar, herded in their thousands, slow and gentle and dim, the beast a southern child first learns to mind. A roast haunch of Bellowback is the Sunday table from Jakupur to the smallest village.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A bellowback herd lay down all at once on the savanna and would not rise until the earthquake had passed.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Bellowback: Bumako
illustration.alt: Broad-bodied Bellowbacks graze beside an adult herder at the jungle’s edge.
illustration.caption: Broad-bodied Bellowbacks graze beside an adult herder at the jungle’s edge.

epigraph.quote: A roast haunch of Bellowback on Sunday, or it isn't Sunday.

title: Cluckmaw
subtitle: Pokok · Table tradition
summary: A small flock-living saurian raised throughout the south for meat and eggs.

sections.title: Form and character
paragraphs: Abundant and domestic, the Cluckmaw is the everyday flock-fowl of the Southern Wilds, kept by households across the region.

sections.title: In southern life
paragraphs: Pokok is its Kalvatari name. Like other saurians, it lays eggs and gives no milk.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Every cluckmaw in a Jakupur village laid an egg with a red speckle on the same morning.” (heard in Jakupur)

source: Bible Complete · Volume XIII, Part Two: The Breeds

illustration.label: Cluckmaw: Pokok
illustration.alt: Small Cluckmaws gather beside a household egg basket in a southern courtyard.
illustration.caption: Small Cluckmaws gather beside a household egg basket in a southern courtyard.
